#3664. Sci-fi RPG Exodus continues evoking Mass Effect by revealing female lead and nicknaming her FemJun

Sci-fi role-playing game Exodus continues to play into the Mass Effect comparisons by revealing the female version of its main character Jun, and with studio Archetype referring to her in marketing material as FemJun.

If that moniker sounds familiar it's because it is: the female Commander Shepard character in the Mass Effect series was nicknamed FemShep. FemShep became an iconic part of BioWare's iconic series, eventually proving that female leads could front games just as successfully as male leads could, and be every bit as popular.

Is the nickname FemJun too blatant? Possibly. But there's well publicised BioWare pedigree at Archetype Entertainment, in the studio's co-founders and in the people leading the project. Key Mass Effect writer Drew Karpyshyn is in charge of writing Exodus, for example, and the similarities to Mass Effect are something the Exodus team has not been shy about in the past. In the wake of Mass Effect 5 being cancelled and BioWare being closed, they become even more alluring.

There are, however, big and important differences between Exodus and Mass Effect, key among them, time dilation. In Exodus, there are special Exodus missions whereby you leave your home planet and fly far away, and in doing so experience time differently to the people back home. Many years will pass for them while few will pass for you, which provides the game with a way to show you long-term consequences of your actions when you return.

Archetype hasn't shown the female version of Jun before, despite having released many videos of Exodus, perhaps to build anticipation for her reveal. It's a press beat that's also provided Archetype - a studio owned by Dungeons & Dragons company Wizards of the Coast - with an occasion to reveal the two actors playing Jun in the game.

Female Jun is portrayed by Carina Conti, who played the lead in the recent Mafia game, The Old Country - Isabella Torrisi. She's appeared in HBO's Winning Time and Hulu/Freeform's Good Trouble as well. Male Jun, meanwhile, is portrayed by Stephen Oyoung, who played Mister Negative in Insomniac's Marvel's Spider-Man 1 and 2 games, and Red Hood in Gotham Knights. He also appeared in Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, The Wrecking Crew, and Twisters. The game also famously stars Matthew McConaughey.

Archetype announced a Dark Horse hardback art book to go on sale alongside the game next year as well. This arrives a week after the game; Exodus arrives 7th April 2027 on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X, and the art book on 13th April.

Matt played Exodus at Gamescom relatively recently and came away impressed, referring to it as "the best kind of surprise". "I wasn't expecting quite such a bombastic 45 minutes when I first picked up a controller and settled into Exodus, admittedly, but the more I played, the more it made sense," he wrote. "I might not be much of a Mass Effect fan (damn you M35 Mako once more), but Exodus is now firmly on my radar ahead of its arrival next year."

World of Warcraft: Forever has a unique problem—it's intended to be a "forever" version of baseline Azeroth, with no planned level-increasing expansions and an emphasis on horizontal progression with only minor vertical item level increases.

But expansion packs are more than just a stack of a few levels, they're also an opportunity to adjust to the MMO economy. Which so often suffers because, well, you're essentially printing money all the time. Every enemy killed, every resource node farmed, every trash item sold, effectively adds more money into the world.

There are ways to remove this money, sure. Repair costs, flight paths, goldsinks like a mount grind, dual spec, or respec fees. But if someone's dedicated to grinding, they can put together a hundred gold in a few hours. Or, in this case, thousands.

As shared by WoWHead, a gold farm was discovered in Blackmaw Hold, one of its new dungeons, and thoroughly rinsed over the past couple of days: "In Blackmaw Hold, there is a room filled with around 30 Blackmaw Devotees. These creatures are non-elites that only auto-attack, but can drop a lot of loot."

All of that loot adds up. Silver drops and vendor items, motes, quest items—and hey, sometimes there's just a good grinding spot in an MMO. I personally made my mount money by rinsing a lucrative little ogre spot with a lot of iron ore. But in that case, I was able to scrape together a humble 15 gold an hour and a half, an honest wage for an honest day's work, whereas these folks have been raking in thousands.

Here's a clip of one such streamer leisurely jogging about with 4,000+ gold in his bags: "I slept for four hours, man, if I didn't sleep, I could've hit 5k."

This is, uh, bad—streamers are in a sense the very tip of the iceberg. If their farming spot has breached containment, then you can bet that ambitious gold sellers and farmers have already been on that grindset for longer. Exactly how much longer is up for debate, mind, since Blackmaw Hold is a high-level dungeon; but these guys are efficient. Even my leisurely pace, taking in the sights, has seen me hit level 51 since launch.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Unsurprisingly, parts of the community are baying for blood: "All of the gold that entered into the economy needs to be removed and everyone involved needs to be banned. This single exploit left unaddressed will affect WoW Forever for its entire lifespan. This gold was created by vendoring items in a raw gold farm. It's gold that was never meant to, designed to, or expected to enter into circulation. Inflation is about to ripple everywhere," writes one player on the WoW subreddit.

Making things slightly more awkward for Blizzard is the fact that the aforementioned streamer I linked above, Ziqoftw, has commentated on PvP tournaments in an official capacity before. He's made the argument on his X account that this wasn't an exploit, and that while the farm was absolutely very lucrative, a hotfix doesn't necessarily mean an exploit happened.

"Hotfixing something because it's too strong or because they don't want players to do it doesn't mean it's bugged, it means that it's too strong," Ziqo writes.

The game's terms of service define "exploits of any in-game bugs, and thereby granting you and/or any other user an advantage over other players not using such methods" as grounds for a ban, so I suppose the question is whether this was considered a bug or not.

On the one hand, it's definitely unintended, otherwise it would've been hotfixed. On the other, MMO players are like water—they'll seep into any weakness your game design has. Should Blizzard have, as Ziqo points out, given this massive group of enemies in a dungeon the exact same loot table as a normal, grindable mob out in the open world? I could probably tell you that's a bad idea.

The question right now is: What the hell does Blizzard do about it? I've reached out to the developer for comment, and I'll update this article if I receive a response.

Harvey's history with games started when he first begged his parents for a World of Warcraft subscription aged 12, though he's since been cursed with Final Fantasy 14-brain and a huge crush on G'raha Tia. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. He also plays a shelf load of TTRPGs in his offline time. Don't ask him what his favourite system is, he has too many.

#3659. Darius Rucker Reflects on ‘Awful’ Divorce From Beth Leonard in Candid Doc

Daris Rucker is opening up about the highs and lows of his life in the spotlight.

“For a lot of years, I experienced some real low lows,” Rucker, 60, shared in his new Hulu documentary Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie. “One of the hardest parts of my life is getting divorced.”

The country singer and ex Beth Leonard announced in July 2020 that they had split after 20 years of marriage. During their relationship, the pair welcomed daughter Daniela in 2001 and son Jack in 2004. (Rucker and his ex Elizabeth Ann Phillips also welcomed daughter Carolyn in 1995.)

“Beth and I stayed together for a lot of years after I stopped partying,” Rucker shared in a new interview featured in the documentary. “I just think we had gotten to a point where the growing apart thing sounds so cliché, but that’s really what it is. It was an awful time.”

The former Hootie and the Blowfish frontman added, “Divorce is awful. It was an awful time, and I look at it as another chapter of life that’s closed.”

In the documentary, old quotes from Rucker appeared on the screen where he discussed the end of his marriage.

“My ex-wife did everything to make my life great,” he once said, “and I did everything in my power to mess it up.”

Although he’s been able to receive a second chance of love by getting engaged to singer Emily Deahl, Rucker still can’t help but feel sentimental when looking back on that admittedly painful chapter of his life.

“I tried to come out of it as a better person and a better dad,” he said in the doc. “It hurts. You feel like a failure, but at some point you have to move on.”

Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie explores the triumphs and hardships that shaped Rucker’s life, from his Charleston, South Carolina, childhood  to global music superstardom. In the project, the “Wagon Wheel” singer gets deeply personal about the cost of fame, revealing his struggles with drugs and alcohol, the breakdown of his marriage and near-death experiences.

Viewers are also treated to candid interviews with friends, fellow musicians and even some family members, like daughter Daniela.

“Still to this day, I don’t really fully have a concept of his fame or his level of fame,” she said when recalling memories of fans approaching her father for photos. “When he gets stopped, when I’m with him … it’s just my dad. But at the time, that was our normal.”

Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie is streaming now on Hulu.

The Governors Awards kick off awards season these days, which means some of Hollywood’s best and brightest trekked across Los Angeles in a bunch of finery to walk the red carpet – or in this case, blue carpet. Some big names from Zendaya to Florence Pugh to Timothèe Chalamet and Glenn Close debuted some memorable celebrity fashion, and I just want to talk about some of the bold looks.

Florence Pugh has been on a very romantic kick lately promoting East of Eden. She’s worn Victorian blouses with big ruffles, and there’s been a lot of puff in her sleeves lately. She did the opposite for the 17th annual Governors Awards. Her satin dress was form-fitting and very different than what we’ve seen her in promoting her Netflix show. But we’re getting close to Dunesday season, baby.

The dress was yet another winner from Valentino, who also made Pugh's infamous sheer dress. I'm still thinking about its ethereal nature.

Charlize Theron also opted for a memorable color. She paired a red curve-hugging dress from Tom Ford with a red lip, and I just can’t stop looking at it. Plus there’s nothing like posing with your dog next to a bathtub to give a little extra allure.

A post shared by Charlize Theron (@charlizeafrica)

Both looks were well-recieved, and lots of fans commented to Charlize with something along the lines of, “Red is definitely your color!” I mean, I can’t disagree with that.

Some did call Zendaya’s brown dress with hip pads “flawless,” while other comments mentioned it’s “giving sophistication and allure." Another post mentioned she could “wear a trashcan” and she’d still look “glamorous.” (Though that’s more of a compliment to Zendaya than the dress.) A subset of people also said Zendaya understood the assignment, as she’s doubtless wearing earth tones to kick off the Dune: Part 3 press tour, but some fans just could not get over the way the dress moved and hung, and the color also seemed to be an issue for some.

Some of the comments about the dress itself noted it was a rare miss in her longstanding collaboration with Law Roach.

Zendaya takes so many fashion risks. She’s done the whole tennis method dressing thing. She once wore a C-3PO armored look and that was seemingly less divisive than this brown dress. I like that she tried something weird with these little side panniers. Despite it being vintage, I’ve certainly not seen much like it on the red carpet, and if this is her kicking off the Dune press tour, it’s certainly a memorable way to begin.

But did it smolder as much as Pugh and Theron? OK probably not.

#3657. ‘La Bola Negra’ Defied Hollywood’s Expectations—and Made Movie Stars out of Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente

In 1936, Federico García Lorca, the Spanish poet and playwright, was working on a new play, La Bola Negra, which was never completed. Only four pages of it were found. Later that year, the 38-year-old homosexual anti-fascist sympathizer was executed during the Spanish Civil War on the orders of right-wing military authorities. Ninety years later, Spanish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi have crafted a new, ambitious film named after these scant remnants. Their glamorous but gritty film stars Spaniards Miguel Bernardeau, of Elite fame, along with Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente, in his first major acting role. La Bola Negra is an epic that spans close to a century; it follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War, all under the shadow of García Lorca’s work.

There are works of art that escape definitions, pieces of media that transcend. La Bola Negra, both the film and the play, is a biography and a document of war; a love story and a tale of generational trauma; an examination of queerness in Spanish history. The film contains stories that speak of fear, of desire, of guilt, and of shame. And it is a work that defies the easy summary of a logline.

“So you would like us to craft that sentence for you,” Bernardeau, 29, says, laughing while sitting next to Guitarricadelafuente at a restaurant in Manhattan. He’s athletic and handsome. He comes across as a classic macho onscreen, perhaps a residue of the characters he’s been cast as, but in person he is softer and warm, thoughtful. His hair is cut in a shaggy semi-mullet, and he’s wearing a Dolce & Gabbana black T-shirt featuring a young Monica Bellucci, a vintage find.

“It’s a movie that when you finish it, it makes you want to live,” Guitarricadelafuente, 29, says. His curly hair spills over his forehead onto his wire-frame eyeglasses. As Guitarrica—a diminutive for guitar in Aragonese (his family has roots in Aragon) and his stage-name shorthand—he sings about romance and sex, mixing the sounds of Spanish tradition with the synths and reverberations of pop. Like Bernardeau, he’s disarmingly attractive, but his persona is more open. Not unlike their characters, Bernardeau appears more stoic, as if he’s standing on firmer ground; Guitarrica is lighter on his feet and bashful, perhaps settling into the newness of being a movie star.

“Not to be dramatic,” Guitarrica continues, “but people, friends that have seen the movie with us, it takes them a moment to compose themselves after,” he says. “Like, fuck, it’s an intense film. I think it makes you want to live and not do anything half-hearted.” Bernardeau looks at his costar with admiration and utters a line from the film: “Nadie desaparece del todo” (No one disappears completely). “It’s a phrase that Rafael says that keeps coming back to me,” he says.

With the enormity of approaching García Lorca, an idol for Spaniards, a paragon for writers, and a hero for queer men, Calvo and Ambrossi (both modern versions of all these things) were not bold enough to attempt to complete La Bola Negra. Instead they built an affecting universe around it, drawing inspiration from it and other works by García Lorca, as well as co-writer Alberto Conejero’s La Piedra Oscura. The latter was itself loosely inspired by Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, a companion of García Lorca and a member of his theater troupe, who died as a soldier during the civil war.

The film tells three stories: that of Sebastián (Guitarrica) in 1937, a young trumpeter taken into the Nationalist army who encounters Rafael (Bernardeau) as a new prisoner put under his watch; of Carlos (Milo Quifes) in 1932, the lead character in García Lorca’s original play and a young gay man who is denied membership to a casino club because of his sexuality; and in 2017, of Alberto (Carlos González), a modern-day historian who, following the death of his grandfather and an excavation into his past, finds himself indelibly connected to the other men. In Carlos’s vignette, club members vote on his admission using black and white balls, where a black ball (la bola negra) signifies a negative. When Carlos receives several, he has to confront his father. The tension between shame and confession becomes the heart of the film.

Sebastián is a character who is, as Guitarrica puts it, “like a custom-made suit” for him. He ran into Ambrossi and Calvo after performing at the Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona two years ago. “It was one of those nights where, after a few drinks, you kind of forget what was said,” he says with a laugh. But he heard from Calvo after that, and soon he was in Madrid meeting with the directors. “I thought they’d ask me to make a song for the soundtrack,” he says. Instead they told him they were writing a film with Conejero, and offered him the role of Sebastián. “I wasn’t confident at all, nothing was clear,” Guitarrica says, “but I saw the faith they had in me.”

Bernardeau, who was invited to audition for Rafael, also had his doubts. “I didn’t think I did well,” Bernardeau says of his audition. “I was like damn, I missed the opportunity of a lifetime.” But after a week and a half of self-inflicted torture, he was asked to read with Guitarrica and was then offered the role. He was sure about his costar: “The choice of Álvaro made perfect sense,” he says.

Bernardeau and Guitarrica were familiar with each other’s work. “But we met as Sebastián and Rafael,” Bernardeau says. These days they appear to have the kind of friendship, of reverence for each other, of two men who’ve gone to war together—even if just on camera.

Despite its hefty emotional punch and astonishing staging, La Bola Negra is a film about war. Human stories are its spoils, and the unrealized potential of lost lives is buried on the battlefields. The Spanish Civil War still looms darkly over the country. Their dead, from unknown soldiers to acclaimed names like García Lorca, have become Spain’s ghosts.

“I felt a ton of responsibility,” Bernardeau says of playing Rafael, with his connection to a real person. “There is a responsibility in telling the story of someone who is no longer here,” he says. “By making this film, I found that he is important to many people, and I didn’t know that.” Bernardeau knew of García Lorca much like anyone who learns about their home country’s foremost literary giants in school, but the life of Rafael perhaps eluded the textbooks. (Ambrossi and Calvo gave him a reading list, and Bernardeau got to work.)

For Guitarrica, the process was more internal. The character of Sebastián was crafted for him, which afforded him the license to find himself in the role, he says, and consider history by imagining what it would have been like to have lived it.

“There was a lot of introspection,” he says. Guitarrica was also learning how to arrive at certain emotions “and unearth my own experiences to be able to give nuance to my character,” he says. Back in Madrid, during that first meeting with the directors, they asked him if he had any emotional traumas. “I said no, and they said, we’ll see,” he says, laughing. Acting, Guitarrica has found, means excavating old wounds. Did he encounter any turmoil? “Well, yes,” he laughs, “but I’m not telling you about that.”

Since the film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May and received a 20-minute standing ovation, with Ambrossi and Calvo winning the award for best direction (alongside Fatherland director Pawel Pawlikowski), Bernardeau and Guitarrica have covered magazines in Spain and beyond and become two of the internet’s latest fixations. La Bola Negra will also represent Spain in the best international feature film category at the Academy Awards, should it be nominated.

“I love that it’s a story that we feel is so ours, that is such a fundamental part of our society and our collective imagination,” Bernardeau says. “The war has impacted us through generations, and it is part of us in different ways.”

He says he doesn’t want to romanticize, but the global reception of such a regional story has given him some faith in humanity. “Because, in the end, it shows that we’re all different, but all the same; that the most personal is also the most creative,” he says, making sure I know that he’s quoting a phrase attributed to Martin Scorsese.

“I think that this film is largely about an idea that is pretty straightforward,” Guitarrica says. “Simply, it’s about the drive to live. Of not leaving anything on the table or unfinished. And that is a very universal story.”

#3656. Booby-Trapped Video Game Console Explodes At Rival Gaming Store

A video game console exploded last month at a repair shop in Santo AndrÃ©, Brazil, injuring two of the people who worked there. Police are calling it an attempted murder, and say a rival business owner was trying to eliminate his competition. The man they think was responsible was arrested over the weekend as part of a separate investigation.

G1 Globo reports (via Dexerto) that the original incident took place on October 23 at around 5:30 p.m. A delivery person dropped off a gaming device for some sort of repair, but inside the retro gaming console, police say there was a concealed timer and two cylinders filled with flammable liquid. The store owner reportedly put the console inside a drawer where it later ignited, putting a hole in the ceiling as well as damaging other parts of the store.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've already had to write the word 'committee' a lot in recent weeks, due to the scandal developing over at Nvidia leading to CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. He's off to see a couple of committees in Congress in coming weeks. Though today it's Nvidia's turn to establish a committee: the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, or NSECOC as I will hereafter call it.

The NSECOC will answer direct to the Nvidia board. It's also led by a board member, Suzanne Nora Johnson, former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs Group. Though the company says it will keep independent experts around for advice and expertise. It will work with the existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team at Nvidia, which will now report to the committee and interim CEO, Colette Kress.

It looks to me like the company's board want to know who Nvidia is sending its GPUs to at all times; something that will be of utmost import in coming months and years as the company's customers have come under recent scrutiny by US lawmakers and agencies. An investigation is being carried out by the US Department of Justice into one of its customers, Megaspeed, the agency confirmed yesterday.

It also means the board has a say in the question of who gets Nvidia's GPUs while the company looks for a new CEO. As it stands, the company's CFO Kress is in the big chair at Nvidia HQ, but the company is looking for a replacement. Recently, Jensen Huang and his allies are said to be floating the idea of him making a return, and his pal president Trump doesn't mind the idea; however, the board isn't considering it according to a source speaking to CNBC.

Nvidia's newly-appointed chairman said of the new committee:

"Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation."

It signs off with a promise to "enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders." Basically, cosy up to the government to keep its business going with minimal disruption or share price drops.

#3654. Nearly a Decade Ago My Friend’s Private Plane Fell Out of the Sky. Then, in Florida This Month, It Happened to Another Friend.

When I was in my late 20s, I lived in the worst building in the best part of SoHo. My apartment above the French restaurant Raoul’s had been created by merging two units, so it was quite spacious. When I decided to move in with my boyfriend in Los Angeles, I still planned to spend a quarter of my time in New York and wasn’t about to give up this gem. But I figured I could find a roommate who would be psyched I wouldn’t be there a ton, and keep the smaller bedroom for myself.

The writer Deborah Schoeneman introduced me to her best friend from Cornell University, who she said would be the perfect roommate. Jen Blumin was a Sex and the City character come to life: a tall, gorgeous blonde who managed a high-end event space with a private pool a few blocks away, mostly for corporate sponsors. I figured she wouldn’t be home much while I was, and told her if she had $1,800 a month, she had a deal. The day she moved in, she gingerly walked up the four flights of stairs carrying a large wrought-iron cage containing a shrieking bird. “Did I not tell you I had a cockatoo?” she asked with such insouciant camp, such mock innocence, that I just had to laugh.

Schoeneman, Grigoriadis, and Blumin in 2010 at Round Hill Resort.

Thus began one of my life’s great friendships, proceeding through many more ripostes, a decade of shared living space, and the birth of two kids each. Jen became wildly successful by turning vacant institutional buildings into heart-stopping event spaces, and even landed the contract for New York Fashion Week at the old post office across from Pennsylvania Station. The love of her life and father of her children, the architect James Ramsey, conceived of an idea with Dan Barasch, another Cornell chum, to create a “low line” under the old Delancy Street trolley terminal, and for a while it seemed like that was going to happen. But the relationship fell apart, and then things move very fast in my memory: Jen started to say she disliked New York City and wanted to live full time in the North Fork, a new boyfriend showed up, now she was moving to Puerto Rico for the climate and tax breaks, then she and the boyfriend were buying a private plane to fly direct from Puerto Rico to Islip, NY.

When I heard about this new acquisition by my far-more successful friend, I have to admit I thought it sounded rad. Private planes occupy an almost mystical place in our culture. You’re up in the skies, free of seatmates chomping tuna sandwiches or annoyances like last-minute checked bags. You’re watching the clouds drift by, close enough to touch God. So what if her plane wasn’t the fanciest! It was still glamorous. As former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown wrote on her Substack, everyone wants to be your friend when you have a plane: “The late TV legend Barbara Walters used to lament the necessity to vacation every year with the crass termagant CEO of a bra company just because said termagant happened to own her own plane.”

For the wealthy, private planes, which have become increasingly popular as a mode of transportation in recent years, aren’t only the ultimate in seclusion, but also the ultimate in spontaneity. You’re in a power position that’s completely the reverse of commercial flights, which reduce you to helpless nose-boned chattel. If you’re paying the bill, most decisions are controlled by you: You decide when you leave, who to invite, what to eat (certainly not pretzels and ginger ale), and whether there’s space for your three bulldogs.

But the day after Mother’s Day in 2017—which Jen memorialized by sending a group text to myself and the core girlfriends with a snapshot of her two toddlers on a big rock in Puerto Rico—Jen’s private plane fell out of the sky. She was flying with her children about 15 miles east of Eleuthera, an island in the Bahamas, in the Bermuda Triangle. None of them were found.

I think a lot about Jen, but rarely more than now, nearly a decade after her death. That’s because this month, the same set of New York friends—loosely—are mourning another person who died with his family, including two more children under five years old. Adam Robinson, who chartered the Learjet that dove into a Florida road on November 1, leaving hypersurreal audio and video recordings that are now seared into the nation’s collective memory, arrived in New York a little later than Jen. I met him in the mid-2000s, but he seemed to be cut from the same cloth as she was: a tall, gregarious Lehman Brothers trader who had inherited a loft on lower Broadway from our mutual friends, the founders of the website College Humor (there was a lot of apartment swapping in lower Manhattan back then).

Adam was the definition of a “good guy”: smart, kind, and wry at the right moments. He had the open-hearted self-possession of someone who had traveled widely, but now he was in New York City to start his career, which, like so many of us, involved being hyper-social. He was not a close friend, but I was always happy to see him, and would usually spend 10 minutes at a crowded party chatting before moving on (this means a lot if you, like me, ascribe to the Fitzgeraldian notion that large parties provide intimacy, and prefer not to waste your breath in this rarefied milieu on dolts). A few guys in the crowd were into email marketing, and I heard that Adam had started a business in that industry but didn’t know much about his life after he moved to Austin, nor that he, too, had become quite successful.

It’s eerie that Adam’s private plane was headed to Eleuthra, the same area where Jen disappeared. But beyond that coincidence, what I keep returning to is how Jen and Adam’s stage in life had so many similarities: both in their 40s, too early to retire, they had nevertheless entered what you could call the “second phase” of success. They weren’t only trying to make money but to enjoy the money they’d made, and for them, that meant devising a new kind of life. Adam had moved from Austin to Aspen and wanted to pursue more outdoor adventures, some of which involved destinations hard to reach by commercial flights. Jen didn’t need to take her fatal private journey—JetBlue flies direct from San Juan to JFK—but having her own plane definitely came with bragging rights, though neither was the type to post a “flashing a peace sign on a PJ” semi-candid shot on Instagram.

And yet the private plane, so much a symbol of freedom and success for both Jen and Adam, led to their demise. This type of aviation is far less regulated than commercial planes, which hew to “strict government regulations enumerated in hundreds of pages of fine print…everything from the stowing of tray tables to announcements concerning lavatory smoke detectors,” as Jeff Wise wrote in Vanity Fair in 2025. That may be okay when you’re traveling in a $75 million G800, or as a guest of Drake in his $185 million plane, or with Kylie Jenner in her $73 million Bombardier, but when you’re on a small plane, it matters. Wise notes in his story that since 2020, almost half of the private plane crashes in the US have been Citations, which are on the smaller side.

And when traveling in a plane that lacks the sophistication of a commercial jet, whether you’re JFK Jr., Aaliyah, or just two people that everyone in a certain downtown Manhattan set knew in the mid-aughts, weather happens. Bad decisions in the cockpit compound, if the pilots even have time to make them. And then everything you’ve worked so hard for is lost, with the wreckage extending to family members and best friends left behind. “If I was Adam, I would rather be on the plane than on the ground” is the refrain I keep hearing from my friends this week, meaning that they’d rather perish with their families than live without them. Success and its luxuries are wonderful things. But they don’t guarantee you’ll get to come home.

Bowen Yang made a surprise cameo on Saturday Night Live this past weekend. The beloved former cast member appeared in multiple sketches, first as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the cold open and later as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in John Mulaney’s wild musical number about New York City. Yang seemed comfortable and back in his element, but it turns out the behind the scenes wasn’t exactly smooth sailing. Sarah Sherman actually had to fill in for him during dress rehearsal, leading to a hilarious visual that’s making the rounds.

Yang is currently crushing it as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway production of Oh, Mary! His schedule on the show, however, isn’t exactly SNL friendly. The Lyceum Theatre offers two performances every Saturday: one at 5 PM and one at 8:30 PM. Since SNL’s dress rehearsal starts at 8 PM, there was no way for the actor to appear in both; so, during the cold open, Sarah Sherman appeared in Yang’s part, hilariously wearing a sign that said Bowen Yang. According to Late Nighter, Marcello Hernández warned the crowd ahead of time, though I can’t imagine they expected this visual, which Yang later posted to his Instagram account…

A post shared by Bowen Yang (@fayedunaway)

It’s unclear exactly when the details of Yang’s appearance came together, but he reportedly did head to Studio 8H after his Broadway show on Friday to do a rehearsal for his two scenes. I can’t imagine longtime showrunner Lorne Michaels would be okay with a random celebrity doing a cameo without the standard rehearsing schedule, but he obviously knows Bowen well enough to know he didn’t need the full runthrough.

He clearly didn’t either, as he was a standout during the live show in both the cold open and as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in the musical number. Saidah Belo-Osagie reportedly played the second part very capably during the dress rehearsal, but that was never going to work for the live show. She had another role in the sketch, and also, Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel was clearly written for Yang, as he’s currently playing Mary Todd Lincoln in the aforementioned show. He probably would have been personally offended if he wasn’t asked and tuned into SNL to see someone else doing an outrageous take on the part he’s currently playing on Broadway.

We’ve gotten two consecutive weeks with cameos from former cast members, as Bobby Moynihan appeared in the Davis S Pumpkins anniversary sketch and in a segment on Weekend Update as Drunk Uncle. Personally, I’d love to see SNL try and do double appearances more often. It’s always fun to see old favorites surprise fans by appearing in a sketch, but it’s even more fun to see those familiar faces show up twice during the same episode so they have a little more to do.

SNL is currently on hiatus for a few weeks, but it’ll return in early December with a new episode hosted by Amanda Seyfried. I cannot wait, as she should bring something new and exciting to 30 Rock and will hopefully continue the momentum as the show has recently dropped its strongest episodes of the season, including this past weekend's heater where John Mulaney brought some of the sharpest social commentary we've gotten in a long time.

#3651. A Ton Of Big Blockbuster Games Are Already On Sale For Black Friday 2026

Black Friday seems to arrive earlier and earlier each year. It’s gone from a single-day event into a month-long deals bonanza where a ton of the discounts are fake. For gaming, the Black Friday “season” is already well underway, and actually a bunch of the deals are pretty good.

Marvel’s Wolverine was a surprising miss for Sony’s first-party PlayStation game factory, but it delivers on spectacle and cinematic comic-book storylines, and it’s currently just $50, which is a very good price for a big-budget blockbuster that came out less than three months ago.

There are a bunch of other recent games that are pretty cheap, too, as well as some older ones:

The other big highlight on this list is 007 First Light, an action-adventure from the makers of Hitman that will probably appear on a bunch of people’s best games of 2026 lists. It’s half off digitally on PS5 right now. Star Wars Zero Company, another strong release this year, is also on sale. Saros, a fairly challenging 3D bullet hell shooter, is more of an acquired taste, but also easy to recommend at just $40.

Final shout-outs go to Borderlands 4 and Mafia: The Old Country. Published by the same company, they couldn’t be more different. Borderlands is a grindy RPG loot shooter with a silly sense of humor. Mafia is a narrative-driven cinematic adventure that you can finish in just 10-12 hours. It’s perfect for people who want a rock-solid game that’s not caught up in all of the minutia and busywork of most modern gaming blockbusters.

At $20 a piece, they’re both a steal. Why so many steep discounts so early in November? Probably to catch your attention before Grand Theft Auto 6 drops in just a few days.

Any way that more efficiently uses cores has the thumbs up from me.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD's Vishal Badole recently posted two Linux kernel patches (via TechPowerUp), and these both pair up to introduce Capacity Aware Scheduling (CAS) for AMD heterogeneous processors. If that sounds like gibberish to you, effectively, this lays the groundwork to more efficiently handle AMD chips that have different core types.

Up until now, AMD's performance scaling driver for Linux (amd-pstate) treated all cores as equal, assigning tasks regardless of core strength. AMD's current heterogeneous design pairs full-fat Zen 5 and lower-caste Zen 5C cores together in Zen 5 chips nowadays, but there is far less actual difference between these two core types than in the P-cores and E-cores of modern Intel architectures.

But Zen 6's full lineup is currently suggested to be quite different. Also shared in a Linux patch earlier this year, Zen 6 is set to introduce a new Low Power core type (which is set to run at a very low power, as you might guess from the name), and that is a core type that would really benefit from Capacity Aware Scheduling.

What AMD has called Performance and Efficiency cores up until now is not the same as what Intel has called Performance and Efficiency cores. AMD's Efficiency cores are effectively just compact versions of the Performance cores, whereas Intel's E and P cores have different microarchitectures and are specifically tailored for different use cases.

The new Zen 6 LP cores appear to be similar to Intel's LPE (Low Power Efficiency) cores you will find in its Panther Lake chips. And as such, the need for CAS makes more sense. If AMD LP cores take after Intel LPE cores, they will be tuned down to run on a very low power limit, so differentiating between cores will allow the system to more efficiently divvy up tasks.

The introduction of CAS isn't just good for the eventual introduction of AMD Zen 6 LP cores (or whatever they will be called when they launch). Badole explained that this change should help even with current heterogeneous processors (Zen 4 and Zen 5). They say, "The scheduler sees every CPU as having identical capacity and treats performance and efficiency cores as interchangeable. Tasks are therefore placed and balanced without regard to core strength, which hurts both throughput and energy efficiency on hybrid systems."

Up until now, the extra efficiency gains from CAS would only be a bonus, but if Zen 6 LP cores are low-power enough, it could be needed for them to operate properly, given what we expect will be a much lower power draw, and therefore much lower performance.

#3649. Scott Colom's Mississippi Is the One You Should Know

“Mississippi is not who you think we are.”

This is what an older Black woman said to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night. The crowd was waiting for Colom to speak after his historic victory, becoming the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction, and its first Democratic senator in nearly a half century. The woman did not give her name, but her simple statement has tattooed itself inside my brain.

“To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment. If you’ve known anyone from Mississippi, you’ve probably heard it. Everyone cites William Faulkner, even though nobody has definitively sourced it. But as the world looks with fresh eyes on my home state, the wisdom checks out.

Onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win. Mississippians are not. The extremes of the moral universe have always been duking it out down there, which makes Mississippi not strange or anomalous, but illustrative.

There’s no avoiding the facts: Human beings have committed the most brutal violence imaginable against their fellow humans in Mississippi, as a matter of law and legacy. One of the consequences of that horror is that it has become prophecy. It is impossible not to feel a sense—from within the state and from without—of frustration and dread that it is taking way too long to emerge from a racism that has raptured the entire culture.

But to people who do not know Mississippians, who do not understand Mississippi—to those who suggest any right-minded or good people simply up and leave, or think the rest of the country should abandon all hope, or worse, look away entirely—you are missing one of the most important threads in the future of American politics and culture. Colom got at this rub when he said that outlets like Cook Political Report, who prognosticate a “solid R” conclusion, are destructive. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote. And if you dismiss possibility in Mississippi, you are compounding the neglect. You are part of the destruction.

You think John McCain was a maverick? Scott Colom is a maverick.

During the race, he drew national attention not only for his prospect of flipping the unflippable, but also because he was doing so through one of the most vivid, creatively engaged, and original campaigns in modern politics. He built a coalition virally, with his twin brother, Andrew Robert Colom, as collaborator, offering “Sheeeeit” to the world (yes, that’s how many white Mississippians really talk), along with a Hollywood-worthy Sinners send-up, and Andrew’s searing spoken-word poem set to the strains of Fannie Lou Hamer. Colom even stood in line at a Trump rally to speak earnestly with voters who would otherwise be against him—I guarantee he won some of them over.

His entire strategy was built on making people recognize Mississippi, in all its underdog idiosyncrasies. He asked Kamala Harris to campaign with him, even as his advisers reportedly told him it would be an error, because he knew she would draw media attention to underfunded hospitals. And he took the phone call informing him that he’d won while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Because we like to laugh in Mississippi, okay?

As Kiese Laymon, novelist, memoirist, and modern-day Mississippi bard, told me, “Once I saw the protein ad, I knew he’d win.”

History doesn’t echo in Mississippi; it rhymes. You can draw a straight line from the murders of Medgar Evers, or those of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, to the killings of Jorge Gomez or Renee Good or Alex Pretti. You can draw a straight line from Theodore Bilbo to Tate Reeves to Donald Trump.

As Kiese wrote in this magazine in 2020, Mississippi politics flow from its culture. (Incidentally, Kiese and Colom both attended Millsaps College, about 10 years apart, and had the same thesis adviser.) In “Mississippi: A Poem, in Days,” Kiese describes how he got into “an altercation with two fraternities on Bid Day”—when the students who want to be in the Greek system receive offers from frat and sorority houses. “Some fraternity members wore Confederate capes, Afro wigs, and others blackened their faces.” They called Kiese and his girlfriend the N-word.

I have never written about the heartbreak of seeing the future governor of Mississippi in that group of white boys, proudly representing the Kappa Alpha fraternity and its confederate commitment to Black suffering. I have never admitted that after playing basketball against Tate all through high school, and knowing that he went to a public school called Florence, not a segregation academy, like so many other white boys we knew, it hurt my feelings to see Tate doing what white boys who pledged their identities to the Old South ideologies were supposed to do.

When I saw Tate in that confederate cacophony of drunken white boyhood, doing what they did, I knew he could one day be governor of Mississippi and president of the United States.

That is still the most damning thing I can ever say about a white boy from Mississippi.

Damning things still happen, and will again. Just days ago, as the votes continued to stack up for Colom, the old ugliness reared its head. White women in my hometown, students at the University of Mississippi, were captured on video making racist gestures—gesturing and making sounds like monkeys—at their Black neighbors’ video doorbell. The school, still embarrassingly insistent on calling itself “Ole Miss,” continues to investigate, while the offenders get so much more grace than they deserve from the victims and their families, as you can see in their CBS interview. I feel deep shame in these moments, because I know this is what so many people think Mississippi is. There is no excuse for it, and no explanation beyond the obvious. The shame should be obvious, too, but a white person from Mississippi is compelled to express it.

The women are not from Mississippi, according to a source familiar; one, Alaina Kunes, is from Wisconsin, where a car dealership that bears her family’s name is now being sued for a separate allegation of racist actions. This is not an excuse, but rather a fear: that Mississippi’s reputation for the worst parts of history continues to attract the worst sorts of people.

But this is partly what Faulkner, or whoever it was, meant by understanding the world through the lens of Mississippi: Everywhere we must hope our better angels prevail.

I was born and raised in Mississippi among a large, politically engaged family who have wanted change for generations. When Sargent Shriver turned up unexpectedly at my grandparents’ house for dinner one night, on a swing through the South in a failed presidential bid, my grandmother whispered the urgent directive of “FHB”—“family holdback”—so her five sons would leave enough food for Shriver. This story, and that guest, was a point of pride her whole life. She was an unforgiving George McGovern campaigner; in our family photo album, among the pool parties and Christmas mornings, are pages of Polaroids she snapped of Richard Nixon’s televised resignation.

Local private schools, as I understood them, were inherently racist. Public school was a choice of one, and I got a world-class education in the Oxford school system. (Hyde-Smith attended Lawrence County Academy and she sent her own child to Brookhaven Academy, both segregation academies.) My class of 2000—I came up with the same kids from kindergarten through high school—was roughly half Black and half white, with the skinniest pie slivers of anything else. I left for college and never moved back, but my parents, brother, and extended family are still there. Today, Mississippi’s public-school students are doing better than most of their peers across the nation; my own children in the New York City school system are getting a more segregated, less excellent education than I did.

My father, a green-energy mayor and a Barack Obama appointee to the Tennessee Valley Authority (fired by Trump amid a Republican board takeover), pushed throughout my childhood to take the Confederate flag off the state flag and to remove the Confederate monument that still mars the Oxford Square. I was about eight years old when someone keyed “LIBERALS” into the trunk of our Honda Civic, probably because of the Ray Mabus for Governor bumper sticker. I recall being worried about it, until I saw that my parents were amused.

As white Southern liberals, we were in a tiny minority. And though the mantle was worn proudly, it was more existential than that—you were proud to be a Democrat not because it was one party over another, but because it was a stand-in for compassion, common good, and humanity. And nowhere could this be truer, or more necessary, than in Mississippi. (By way of disclosure, I see no conflicts in telling you all this. As former Time editor Rick Stengel says, “You should be non-partisan, but not neutral. Journalists must be biased in favor of the truth and facts. Biased in favor of democracy itself.” And this is the truth, in favor of democracy.)

Scott Colom and I were born a year apart in the earliest 1980s, during a sort of second-wave new New South rebranding. More jobs were coming into the state thanks to manufacturing; more national attention was being paid to Black Mississippians’ cultural contributions (the Delta Blues Museum was established in 1979). William Winter was governor the years of our respective births, and he gave us free kindergarten. William Allain, whose moment was virtually destroyed by a racist, homophobic GOP slander campaign, followed. And Allain was succeeded by Mabus—who won on the slogan “Mississippi will never be last again.” Now, with the exception of Ronnie Musgrove, the governor has been a Republican since 1992. We’ve never had a Black person, or a woman for that matter. Have you had many good thoughts about Mississippi in all this time? I don’t think you have.

Heavy, Kiese’s devastating and raw memoir of coming of age as a Black boy in Mississippi, written in address to his activist and educator mother, gives his own view into 1980s and ’90s Mississippi: “You worked on Governor Mabus’s campaign and kept talking about how much was possible politically in Mississippi because it was the blackest state in the nation,” he writes. And his mother says to him: “Do you understand what’s possible if we actually get effective radical politicians in place down here?” Kiese responds, “I’m glad Mabus won but hearing about it every day is just kinda mee-guh.” Meager. It was not enough then, and we have plenty far to go.

Heavy was published in October 2018, just before Stacey Abrams turned Georgia purple, signaling to the rest of the country that it was time to take notice of the deeply disenfranchised Southern states.

When I reached out to Mabus, who went on to become Bill Clinton’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and then Obama’s Secretary of the Navy, he identified the dominoes that knocked toward Colom’s win: the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, rampant corruption, a welfare scandal featuring Brett Favre, and “office holders taking constituents for granted” over decades. Mabus was a young man working for Winter when Colom and I were little, and this election, he said, “brings hope for the future.”

It doesn’t really matter which party you’d like to claim. Repulsive policies will eventually push everyone away. Mississippi Republicans are not moderate, are not descended of gentle governance. (See: Bilbo et al.) This is the state that put “personhood” on the ballot as part of a national antiabortion strategy; fortunately for all y’all, Mississippians rejected the idea of life beginning at conception. Lynn Fitch, the current attorney general, not only effortfully attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, but she is the signed counsel for the petitioners in the Dobbs brief, which ultimately reversed Roe v. Wade. (Because I keep underscoring to you the infinite refractions of Mississippi, Fitch also went after Colom for one of his ads that used AI; he removed it.) Even the affidavit ballots that have taken so long to count are a result of strident, generational attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise Black voters. Which is why Mississippians knew, as the Colom–Hyde-Smith race came down to those affidavits, exactly in whose favor they would tally up. Were it not for the dedication of young Black canvassers—especially Black women—and homegrown mobilization efforts, things would have gone differently.

“There is a radical history of Black academics, activists, lawyers, and judges who have really been working to see a Mississippi where this was possible,” Kiese emailed me over the weekend. “I am thankful that someone like Leslie McLemore, who was a young member of Hamer’s Mississippi Democratic Party, can see what they worked and died for.”

What does Colom’s win mean for Kiese? “It means that the people, not any party, get what they organize and fight for,” he replied. “Our state taught the world that again last week.”

My privileged position occluded my own understanding of Mississippi’s true potential until I was older. Growing up, I mostly just clocked defeat—every presidential election, every midterm, Mississippi was red as red could be, as Mississippi’s poverty levels ratcheted toward a 21st-century high of 24%. In 2008, John McCain beat Barack Obama in the state by a 13% margin (the two staged a debate in Oxford). In 2016, Trump bested Hillary Clinton by almost 18 points.

After Trump won in 2024, an old childhood friend who’d gone MAGA texted me a GIF of a penis ejaculating stars that reconstituted in the shape of a patriotic eagle. Flash forward a year later, he’s angry about gas prices, and, more striking to me, horrified by the war in Gaza. Colom’s protein ad is for him, and that nerve of enthusiasm it struck is going to keep firing.

Colom didn’t run on pronouns or any numerical strain of woke. He has said he is a fan of Trump’s border security, agrees with him on certain tax policies, and supports the Second Amendment. When asked about improving wages for government employees, he has said he wants to take care of teachers—and cops. As Colom told Jen Psaki in a televised interview, “We gotta be a party that represents our whole country, that understands all parts of the country.”

Now that people outside Mississippi are waking up to Colom, leftists may find his centrism irritating or even offensive. You may find a new reason to look down your noses at Mississippi. It all but promises to provide an opportunity.

So I will just leave you with the brothers Colom.

“They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state, but the cotton cow fed the nation. Europe eating off the same plate. They lied about Mississippi. Said the torture was only here, but the banker’s desk in northern mills still dripping blood from hostage tears. They lied to us all. That’s propaganda machine on both sides, running on slander…. Denying the nation condoned it, denying the nation owned it, denying the nation fed off pain…. They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state.”

He says, invoking Hamer, “Mississippi Freedom Party began again.”

And the vision of Scott: “There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed by what’s right.”

#3648. Stars Who Have Played James Bond Over the Years

James Bond is one of the most iconic characters in cinematic history — and yet, only a handful of actors have been fortunate enough to tackle the part.

The popular action film franchise is based on a character created by author Ian Fleming for his James Bond book series. EON Productions gained the rights to distribute all related movies in 1962, beginning with Dr. No.

Pierce Brosnan, Timothy Dalton and Roger Moore are among those who have served as the British spy. However, Sean Connery has often been regarded as the best actor to step into the role.

When he died in October 2020 of respiratory failure, fellow Bond actor Daniel Craig praised Connery for the way he “defined an era and a style” with his take on the character.

“The wit and charm he portrayed onscreen could be measured in megawatts; he helped create the modern blockbuster,” the Logan Lucky actor said in a statement on the official 007 website. “He will continue to influence actors and filmmakers alike for years to come.”

Craig, for his part, took his fifth and final leap as Bond in 2021’s No Time to Die after 15 years in the role. In November 2026, Robert Pattinson was officially cast as the new 007.

Sing Sing was one of my favorite movies of 2024 and one of the best movies of that year. Colman Domingo shines. He once again proves that he’s one of the best actors of his generation. Domingo’s brilliant scene partners, many not professionally trained actors, magnify his performance.

Using former Sing Sing Prison inmates, and some of those the story was based on, was a revolutionary idea. When I saw Union County, I became more convinced that films should enlist locals or real-life inspirations so those stories appear as characters in more films.

Will Poulter plays Cody, a man in a court-ordered recovery program in Union County. He’s doing fairly well in it until he reunites with his foster brother Jack (Noah Centineo). The film depicts both of their struggles to stay sober, while also highlighting these recovery programs and the people who use them. I first saw Union County at the Davis Theater in Chicago at a special screening with Poulter in attendance.

He explained his experiences with making the movie and having real people from Union County in it. You feel that community throughout. It, in a way, makes Union County feel more grounded in reality than other films with similar topics.

Addiction and recovery are popular subjects in art. Union County may be among the best films about addiction because it feels intimate and quiet while honestly and organically tackling addiction and recovery. Director Adam Meeks puts respect and care into the film’s authenticity and highlights the community without judgment.

I love hearing filmmakers, actors, and creatives speak about their work. You get a better understanding of the process and intentions behind things. You also get a firsthand look at the passion for the project. Therefore, I enjoyed hearing Poulter speak about the importance Meeks and he put into their work with the community. Someone in the audience at the Davis Theater showing knew a person who appeared in the film. She therefore further highlighted how the community bonded even more while making Union County.

Many actors carry the prejudgment that they don’t like working or associating with those outside the acting and filmmaking world. Therefore, it is refreshing to see and hear about those who care about working with all scene partners, whether they’re an extra or an Oscar-winning actor, with the same courtesy, respect, and compassion.

Union County digs into the many aspects of addiction, including mental health. It’s another very honest movie about the mental struggles of addiction. Effectively showcasing things like the mental health struggles of addiction likely comes from consulting those with addiction while creating this film.

Besides Poulter and Centineo’s brilliant performances, Union County gets a lot of its power and authenticity from the people in the community playing extras or small roles. They don’t feel like people playing a part but those putting their real life on the screen in one way or another. It’s these types of lived experiences that make movies such as Sing Sing and Union County unique but also profound.

Many movies are all about escapism, while others remind you of the tragedy and hope of everyday life. The latter films often stay with you longer. It’s more transformative when those who understand the experience of the characters personally participate in the making of movies.

Spent most of my life in various parts of Illinois, including attending college in Evanston. I have been a life long lover of pop culture, especially television, turned that passion into writing about all things entertainment related. When I'm not writing about pop culture, I can be found channeling Gordon Ramsay by kicking people out the kitchen.

#3646. Fan-Made Saga Of Tanya Doujin Game Ignites Controversy After Going On Sale

Can you make money on a fan work? The question constantly bubbles under the gray area of Japan’s doujin sceneâfan groups that create fan worksâencompassing hobbyist manga and games sold at in-person fan events like Comiket. While some of these projects can be entirely original (doujin work is not always derivative, but rather anything created by and for fellow fans), many are based on popular IP, and exist because major companies often overlook or allow their existence, provided they don’t overstep certain boundaries while infringing on IP, that is. Which is why some fans reacted strongly to the news that one developer, working on a 3D action game using characters from the Saga of Tanya the Evil anime, planned to sell digital copies of its work on its official store. The resulting response has led the developer to cancel online sales.

The Saga of the Sky Front, based on the popular long-runningÂ Saga of Tanya franchise, faced controversy after the devs attempted to make money from the game online. The game is a third-person aerial shoot ’em up in which you control the titular Tanya flying via her famous hoverboots, zipping through the skies in dogfights with other soldiers. I was recently at the Digital Games Expo in Akihabara, Tokyo where a demo of the game was being showcased, and found it to be a relatively interesting aerial action game.

With development on the gameâs beta now complete, creator PomyGames chose to sell this initial version of the game on its own digital storefront for 300 yen (about $2), with a physical copy costing 1000 yen (about $6). Whereas in-person sales can often be overlooked by rights owners due to their limited availability, with profits primarily going toward manufacturing and the cost of renting a space at a convention, the decision to sell online is what led many to speak out against the creator.

One user felt the the game went too far in associating itself with the original creators. âIncluding the series name is one issue,” they wrote on X, “but I think listing the authorâs name on the store page was the biggest mistake [made in selling this game].â Others pointed out the risk of it being confused for an official work. âThe problem is that the chance of a rights holder intervening and blocking the sale of a fan game is much higher than it is for a doujin manga,â said one. âIt has a risk of being mistaken as an official game adaptation, and thereâs the chance it could harm [official publisher] Kadokawaâs profits if they choose to release a game with the same concept.â

If a series explicitly allows fans works, often the sale of said worksâeven onlineâcan be permitted in select circumstances provided they don’t attempt to be seen as an official work. Some IP holders may put specific conditions on derivative works, with the expectation that fans will adhere to the rules. For example, Uma Musume creator Cygames notes that, while fans can create doujin, they are not allowed to create adult sexual works, in part due to the characters being based on real horses. One doujin creator summed it up well: âThe reason doujin tend to be allowed to exist is that they often consist of what-if scenarios that authors would like to see, but would probably not feature in the original work, meaning they donât compete with the core media. However, even if it was a doujin work, if someone wanted to create and sell a manga that was in a style that could be mistaken for the original and could be viewed as a potential continuation of that story, the chance people would intervene could increase greatly.â

This is where the line was crossed in the eyes of many, leading the creator to pull the game from sale. Without permission from the rights holders, it can feel against the spirit of doujin to create something like this, regardless of a fanâs intentions.

There's a laundry list of things people are excited to do in Grand Theft Auto 6 once it finally releases in a couple of days. Perhaps you want to know what a loving relationship feels like, maybe you're just concerned about what kind of cars you'll be able to drive around in, or it could be that all you want to do is go bird watching.

Well it really does seem like the sky's the limit in GTA 6, because you can do all three of those things; the healthy relationship will take some extra work though. During a recent interview with The Guardian, Rob Nelson, co-head of Rockstar North explains that players will have a wildlife logbook, which includes 62 different species of birds, for those who want to see all the wildlife Leonida has to offer.

Aside from the gull that was mentioned in the interview, I'm not aware of which specific birds can be found in GTA 6. Actually I don't even know what gull was sighted. It could have been a laughing gull, a herring gull, or perhaps a small ring-billed gull. I'd say the possibilities are endless but they aren't. Officially, 529 species of bird can be found in Florida as of 2019, so 62 is but a fraction of that number.

It's probably a safe bet that we'll see a bald eagle and the american flamingo in GTA 6, but I personally hope to find a snowy plover or perhaps a swallow-tailed kite, but I'm not holding my breath.

Aside from birds, Leonida will be full of all sorts of other species, over 170 according to GameInformer. There's going to be manatees, pelicans, alligators, green iguanas, cane toads, and even a few rhesus macaque monkeys. So by the sounds of things twitchers and other fans of wildlife watching will have heaps to do in GTA 6, besides all the crime and driving, that is.

#3644. Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Makes a Weak Case for His Post-Trial Comeback

For weeks, Los Angeles has been plastered with posters of a malevolent-looking man in a top hat and gray sideburns. It always takes me a few minutes to process that this elderly curmudgeon is Johnny Depp, doing his Hollywood walk of shame in Ebenezer.

“It’s good to be back,” Depp gurgles in the movie’s trailer. He’s either reveling in his return from infamy or trolling the audience, depending on your point of view.

I adored Johnny Depp back in his Edward Scissorhands/Gilbert Grape/Ed Wood heyday; he probably would’ve been my hall pass if I’d known about the concept back then. Now, though, it feels as if the once chiseled-cheeked heartthrob has found a character that suits him: a monstrous figure seeking redemption.

“Grant me the grace to prove that I am no longer the man that I once was,” Ebenezer Scrooge begs one of the ghosts haunting him in this rather plodding new version of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, directed by horror auteur Ti West. Scrooge is trying to make up for a lifetime of stinginess and cruelty, whereas Depp seeks to win back mainstream audiences after the ugly, drawn-out brawl that was his marriage and divorce from Amber Heard.

Heard alleged that he was an abusive addict. Depp denied abusing her and filed two defamation suits. He aimed one at the British tabloid The Sun for calling him a wife-beater (which he lost, since the court found the characterization to be “substantially true”). The other was leveled at Heard for describing herself in a Washington Post op-ed as “a public figure representing domestic abuse.” What started as a defamation trial ended up as a livestreamed referendum on post-#MeToo gender politics.

The saga spawned organized smear campaigns soaked in misogyny. Social media erupted with vile memes, hashtags, and videos targeting Heard, bearing hashtags like #AmberHeardIsAPsychopath and #DontBelieveAllWomen. One men’s group launched a “Ditch the Witch” protest in support of Depp. It seemed to echo one of Depp’s texts about Heard, released during the trial, in which he proposed to a friend: “Let’s drown her before we burn her!!!…I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she is dead.” And it wasn’t just ordinary guys taking up arms for Depp. Moments after the verdict was announced, the GOP’s House Judiciary tweeted a GIF of Depp in Pirates of the Caribbean from its official account, showing support for him.

“The craziness [aimed at Heard] was a kind of pent-up anger at women,” a film producer suggested to me back in 2022. “I think it really stirred up a lot of deep-seated resentment that hasn’t been allowed expression since #MeToo.”

Depp didn’t come out of the crucible with his career intact. He was asked to resign from the Fantastic Beasts franchise—though Warner Bros. still paid Depp his full $16 million salary—and his former agent claimed Disney dropped him from the next Pirates of the Caribbean movie. Still, he never really went away. In fact, like so many guys who have been supposedly “canceled,” he wormed his way back in quite easily. In 2023, he got a standing ovation at Cannes for his role as Louis XV in the French film Jeanne du Barry. The next year, he directed the movie Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness. Meanwhile, producer Jerry Bruckheimer confirmed in 2025 that he’s been talking to Depp about a sixth Pirates film after all. All the while, Depp has also kept his massive brand deal as the face of Dior’s Sauvage.

“I don’t feel boycotted by Hollywood because I don’t think about Hollywood,” Depp announced imperiously a few years back. “I don’t have much further need for Hollywood.” Enter Ebenezer, his official return to…Hollywood. Which he doesn’t need or think about. At all.

Call it Christmas-washing: What could be more wholesome and uncontroversial than A Christmas Carol? According to Variety, Paramount paid Depp just $5 million—a big drop-off from the days when he could reportedly command $50 million for a single film—and only spent $38 million to produce the movie, hedging its bets. Still, this film is a pretty warm welcome back to American movie screens, major marketing campaign and all.

Unfortunately, Depp’s mediocre performance in Ebenezer doesn’t dispel the sour scent of desperation that hangs over his career. Scrooge is one of the most unlovable characters in all of literature, and Depp’s charm does not shine through the gnarled facial prosthetics. He plays the archetypal miser in the broadest of ways, spending much of the nearly two-hour movie alternating between exaggerated expressions of cantankerousness and horror. Depp’s inspiration for the role might as well have been Oscar the Grouch, though one with less educational value who’s hollow at his core. At various points, the actor campily throws himself into physical comedy that is at odds with the horror-soaked vibe of West’s production.

Knowing this is a test run for Depp’s uncanceling, viewers will find it hard not to see Ebenezer as a wink-filled plea for absolution. “I’m not the man I was!” his character screams over and over. “Allow me my redemption.” To which the answer—or my answer, at least—is simple: Bah, humbug.

At first, I thought I was the only one ready to retire the jeans-and-boots combo. Then, I looked at celebrities, rich New Yorkers and posh moms in my neighborhood. Turns out, boots are stale, and loafers are the luxe, trendy alternative to wear with jeans. I found 13 chic pairs that nail the aesthetic, all inspired by styles I see on the classiest ladies in town. The best part? They start at only $10!

Unlike boots, which only really work with tailored denim, these sophisticated loafers stun with every cut, from wide to baggy to barrel. You can even wear them with cropped jeans. And for those wondering about comfort, you’re in good hands. I refuse to wear uncomfortable shoes — so yes, these fall loafers are incredibly plush and supportive. Let’s jump in!

1. Totally Timeless: Everyone needs staple loafers, and this timeless pair is yours. They could totally pass for real leather, especially with the shiny gold hardware that makes them double luxe.

5. Bestselling Hybrid: Something between loafers and flats, these pointed shoes go from coffee-shop-casual to office-polished with a quick change of pants. Over 9,800 five-star ratings don’t lie!

6. European Vibes: An intricate penny strap gives these Lifestride London loafers a European flair, as does the perfect 1.25-inch heel height. They offer a mini boost without the ache.

7. Center of Attention: I’ve been searching (and searching) for shoes to wear with my holiday dresses, and these festive red loafers check every box, with a vibrant hue and a shiny finish.

8. Quiet Luxury: Boutiquey and relaxed, these genuine suede slip-ons are guaranteed to garner compliments. Together, the cute bow, contrast stitching and low profile whisper ‘quiet luxury.’

9. Classy Croc: Make a statement in these croc-embossed loafers. They give any outfit a sassy, high-end twist, be it a tee and jeans or a fancy dress.

10. Colors Galore: My fall wardrobe is filled with neutrals, which is why these glossy pink shoes caught my eye. The color pairs oddly well with black and brown, adding a subtle pop of personality without leaning spring.

11. Trendy Tortoise: Everything about these tortoise-style loafers is elevated, including the structured shape, delicate bow and mirror-like sheen that’s so lustrous, you could probably check your lip gloss.

12. Worth It: Steve Madden is a staple brand of mine, but these cow-print loafers? Totally out of my comfort zone. Rich moms are embracing the trend, though, so I’m tempted to join the club.

13. East Coast: It’s hard to believe these nautical shoes are only $10, but I’m not complaining! They’re what happens when loafers meet boat shoes — and they’re as dreamy as they sound.

YES! There are spoilers below for You Can See Everything, which you can still catch in theaters as part of the 2026 movie schedule.

Now that the cat is officially out of the bag regarding Amanda Seyfried’s surprise role in the hit A24 release You Can See Everything, I’ve been waiting to hear from Christopher Abbott. The East of Eden star plays Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, in the recreations that Seyfried is also a part of. Like so many spoilers in the movie, the cast and crew have been pretty mum about the production. Finally, we’ve heard from Abbott.

Abbott has been very busy over the last couple of years with projects like Wolf Man and The Testament of Ann Lee, plus his Tony-nominated performance in Death of a Salesman on Broadway this year. He's been a little overshadowed in the hype around You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Seyfried’s appearance is such a WTF moment that, speaking as an audience member, it’s almost like we were all still processing that to even register Abbott’s cameo as Evans. It took a couple of minutes before I put it together, honestly. Abbott himself admitted to the process being rushed for him, as well, telling The Hollywood Reporter:

Nathan and Lance, not that long before I went to go work on [it], had just called me and asked me to come mess around. I got to see some of the footage that they had shot before.  I did it, so you know, it was a very kind of quick run-and-gun thing for me, at least.

Abbott also revealed that because it was so quick, he didn’t have a lot of time to prepare or study the character and relied on the footage that Fielder and Oppenheim shot while they were embedded with Holmes and Evans before the former Theranos fraudster reported to prison in 2023. Of the prep, Abbott says:

I've been a fan of both of them for a long time, so I kind of said yes before they even told me what they wanted to do. For me, it was just sort of fun to not to make it so basic. I didn't really know of him until they showed me the footage from the thing. So I just thought it was a very interesting character. I didn't dive deep. I sort of had just enough time to maybe try to do some version of mimicry or find little nuances.  He's an interesting subject.

I think part of what makes it work so well in the box office hit is that we, as an audience, like Abbott, weren’t really familiar with Evans. By the time Abbott appears, we know as much about Evans as he did when he took the role. He’s playing the same villainous character we’ve seen over the previous two hours of the movie, and it works really well.

Abbott probably won’t get any Oscar buzz like Seyfried is getting, but that’s not a slight on him in the least. He provides another bonkers moment in a movie full of them. I really can’t wait for this movie to hit streaming so I can really dive back into it and his performance.
