#3563. As MAGA Melts Down, MAHA Is Also Breaking Apart—Starting With the Moms

In August 2024, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suspended his presidential campaign and endorsed Donald Trump, bringing his ragtag bunch of supporters—crunchy mamas, anti-vaxxers, and conspiracy theorists; testosterone bros, peptide enthusiasts, and people who put a “COEXIST” bumper sticker on their car in the 1990s—along for the ride. But now that the blue wave or tsunami—pick your tortured water metaphor—has come to pass, the fractures within MAHA threaten to break the movement apart, driven by bitter disappointment with the Trump administration.

“I think we are seeing a fracturing of the MAHA movement as those concerns start pulling people in different directions,” says Sandro Galea, dean of the Bursky School of Public Health at Washington University in St. Louis. Groups that are interested in healthier food are not necessarily the same as groups opposed to vaccines, he points out; it’s not a sure thing that those groups will continue to find common cause.

The crack-up didn’t start with the midterms, though the fact that most MAHA-backed candidates lost certainly accelerated it. Earlier this year, Trump had to withdraw his nomination of MAHA darling Casey Means for surgeon general after her stance on vaccines made it impossible for Republicans to get enough votes to support her confirmation. In May, MAHA ally Marty Makary, the commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, resigned, reportedly because of pressure from the administration to authorize fruit-flavored vapes. And in October, Calley Means—Casey’s brother—resigned from his high-level post under Secretary Kennedy at Health and Human Services, with MAHA outrage on unmet promises growing.

Three days after the midterms, Joe Rogan released a bomb-throwing, names-naming, two-plus-hour interview with Calley Means, in which the former Kennedy adviser used the word “demonic,” possibly in the literal sense, eight times.

The big takeaway was that Susie Wiles seemed to have told Kennedy to go sit in a corner and play by himself. All roads to Trump went through her office, and according to Means, she slow-walked, watered down, or outright quashed many MAHA priorities. According to Means, she did this primarily because of her and her family’s financial ties to lobbying on behalf of big business.

Wiles did not respond to a request for comment, but a spokesperson for Wiles previously told Axios that these allegations were “outrageous, defamatory, and provably false.”

Means argued that MAHA managed some wins: Trump signed an executive order to boost research on the use of psychedelics for treating mental health conditions. The new food pyramid instructs Americans to eat more steak than oatmeal. (In this economy?) There have been other MAHA victories too: The administration made it easier for Americans to get a handful of unproven injectable peptides, including the “Wolverine stack.” Trump signed an executive order in support of regenerative farming. The administration requested changes to the labels on testosterone products in an effort to make the hormone easier to prescribe—good news for Pete Hegseth’s promise of a “high-T Department of War.” It asked food manufacturers to voluntarily phase out some food dyes. It has sought to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines.

Means did not cite the United States recently losing its measles-elimination status as a win, though that was also a result of MAHA talking points.

The MAGA-MAHA mind meld provided plenty for the wellness bros, but precious little of what MAHA moms were expecting from their alliance with Trump. Tiffany Cianci, a high-profile MAHA advocate who goes by @thevinomom on Instagram, says the results were “small things,” not the massive systemic changes that had been promised.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for HHS pushed back on this narrative, writing, in part, “HHS has delivered the most sweeping public health reforms in modern history…Across the federal government, the administration has transformed food and nutrition policy, invested more than $1 billion in regenerative agriculture and farm modernization, and taken action to address harmful chemical exposures.”

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivers remarks during an event at HHS in August. The event highlighted a series of 'landmark actions' to improve the nation's food.

For the MAHA moms, there are two original sins of Trump 2.0. The first is the administration’s outright support for glyphosate, an herbicide that has been classified as a probable carcinogen by a World Health Organization agency. The second is its failure to put out a definition of ultra-processed foods, which the movement sees as the first step toward curbing those foods, particularly in school lunches. One was never released; Means alleged to Rogan that ultra-processed-food initiatives such as this were stymied by White House officials including Wiles, who he said told him, “I need sugar money.” Reporting found that food CEOs leaned on the White House to make the definition go away.

A White House official said on background that the definition for ultra-processed food remains a priority and is actively being worked on by relevant agencies. White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said that “the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump…The administration has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

However, the Trump administration has arguably hindered research on ultra-processed foods in other ways. A leading scientist who was studying ultra-processed food’s link to diabetes and obesity took early retirement from the National Institutes of Health last year after NIH officials, he said, censored the reporting of some of his study results because the study didn’t prove the hypothesis of ultra-processed-food addiction as they had hoped it would. If he’s to be believed, one of our best hopes for understanding the health risks of ultra-processed foods exited due to the actions of MAHA officials. (Vanity Fair has reached out to HHS for comment on the allegations of censorship; an HHS spokesperson previously told The New York Times, “NIH scientists have, and will, continue to conduct interviews regarding their research through written responses or other means. We remain committed to promoting gold-standard research and advancing public health priorities.”)

“We do have a food supply that’s nearly 70% ultra-processed food,” says Jessica Knurick, a registered dietitian and science communicator on social media. She counters that many of MAHA’s alleged priorities are aligned with the hopes of public health workers and nutritionists—yet the movement writ large has eroded trust in the very professionals who do that work. “They really want fewer environmental toxins. If you want that, you need strong regulation on corporations,” she says. “They voted in an administration that is decisively deregulatory.”

“All of the things that the MAHA movement claimed to have wanted,” she adds, “this administration has legislated in the exact opposite direction.”

See, for instance, the glyphosate debacle. Instead of curbing the herbicide, something for which he’d long been an advocate, Kennedy got on board with Trump’s support of it, including an executive order that actually prioritized production of the chemical under the bizarre guise of national security. Then the administration supported Roundup weed killer manufacturer Monsanto, now owned by Bayer, in a case before the Supreme Court, which resulted in a decision shielding the company from state-level lawsuits brought by those who believed they’d been harmed by the glyphosate-containing product. (Glyphosate-based Roundup products are no longer produced for the US residential market.)

This flew in the face of everything MAHA believed about Kennedy’s priorities. Vani Hari, a MAHA influencer who goes by the Food Babe, has been called both the Jenny McCarthy of food and a Democratic infiltrator. She thinks that the last nearly two years resulted in some positive change. She also tells me that she’s become somewhat disillusioned: “There have also been deeply disappointing decisions, particularly when it comes to glyphosate and pesticides.”

Despite it all, the HHS secretary continues to be deified by the vast majority of MAHA leaders, who don’t blame Kennedy for these setbacks. Cianci, however, blames just about everyone involved. “What I see within MAHA right now is a fracturing into one very, very small sliver that loves the proximity to power and the fundraising. They unfortunately tied their hitch to the wrong horse, which is partisanship,” she says. “And you have the rest of us that actually want our kids to be healthy.”

Supporters of the Make America Healthy Again movement are seen at a news conference on removing synthetic dyes from America's food supply, at the Health and Human Services Headquarters in Washington, DC, 2025.

If there is a road forward for MAHA, it might be best exemplified by Elizabeth Frost, a community health advocate and the leader of MAHA Ohio. She comes by her skepticism of the pharmaceutical industry honestly, after growing up in Appalachian Ohio during the height of the opioid epidemic. She now runs a political consultancy in the state, which she says works with both parties.

Beginning last year, Frost partnered with epidemiologists from Yale to find out how the people of East Palestine, Ohio, were still being affected by toxic exposures after the 2023 derailment of a train filled with hazardous materials. Frost went to bat for the scientists, lending her local grassroots credibility to their study on water quality in the town.

“I think there is a broader anti-corporate movement in America that hasn’t really been given a home with either established party because both parties have their own pet corporate interests,” she tells me. After Kennedy’s ascent, she had hoped for a focus on the MAHA issues that enjoy broad support. “Vaccines are not the most popular issue even for MAHA. Most people in MAHA would prefer for the majority of time to be spent talking about issues that are a little bit more unifying”—rather than something like Steak ’n Shake’s now using beef tallow for its french fries. “It’s just not where people’s hearts are.”

Speaking of no heart: Stephen Miller has been promoted to chief of staff after Wiles was forced out in the wake of the midterms. Both Calley Means and Secretary Kennedy have celebrated the move. “Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken,” Kennedy wrote on X.

But some MAHA moms are not so sure about the kraken. Cianci says that within MAHA, “people are very, very, very uncomfortable” with Miller. “If you’re just going to do what you’ve been told to do and take it to the extreme—he’s like the human embodiment of the paper clip problem,” she says.

Frost is similarly concerned about how things might go under Miller. “I don’t expect that on environmental exposures, industrial contamination, a strong streak against corporate influence—I doubt we’re going to get those things,” she says. She is also dismayed by MAHA leadership’s embrace of convicted rapist Russell Brand. “What the hell are we doing?” she wonders.

A person familiar with MAHA thinking who spoke on background counters that while it’s fair to say that Miller might be polarizing, he is also not beholden to corporate interests the way Wiles was, making him far less likely to block the scrutiny of pesticides and healthy food policies.

Cianci, Frost, and Hari all hope that MAHA will survive by focusing on policy over partisanship. “I also believe MAHA’s future must be bipartisan,” Hari wrote in an email.

Cianci sees opposition to data centers as the next big issue on which MAHA can lead. And she hopes that the anti-corporate tilt she sees in MAHA will spread. “We had a record number of candidates get elected to Congress this year that turned down all corporate PAC money. That is indicative of the MAHA movement. That is indicative of anti-corruption. And I think they’re going hand in glove.”

Frost would like to see Republicans work with progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on shared goals, like getting pesticides out of the food supply. She wants legislators to realize that “the way to hold their seat is to work across aisles on issues that their constituents care about.”

Perhaps MAHA can reinvent itself by leveraging some of its most popular issues to make common cause with Democrats. After all, 30% of midterm voters told pollsters that they support the MAHA movement, while many more—the vast majority of Americans—say that food additives and pesticide use should be more regulated. A plurality of Americans do not want data centers in their communities. The movement’s best hope for staying relevant is probably the (currently very pissed) MAHA moms, whose concerns about food and pollution were always the most broadly resonant parts of the MAHA platform—rather than a yen for peptides, beef tallow, or testosterone.

Most people want to be able to afford healthy food and effective health care. Trump’s rule has not made those things more accessible, with high cost of living, massive cuts to Medicaid, the ending of certain Affordable Care Act subsidies, and reductions in federal funding for SNAP benefits.

The challenge with a rebrand is that the connection to MAGA is right there in the name. But Trump’s presidency clearly has a shelf life, and MAHA wants to outlast him. “If anyone has any ideas on how to change the name of a political movement,” Frost says, “let me know.”

#3562. An NES Power Glove Just Became The Most Dangerous Weapon In Pro Wrestling

All Elite Wrestling's recent Full Gear event had no shortage of great moments, but Austin Creed stole the show with a move straight out of Street Fighter. After teaming up with his Next Level partner Kofi Kingston and Swerve Strickland to take on Bandido, Hangman Adam Page, and Brody King in a Texas Death Match, anything went in this brawl — including vintage NES accessories.

Looking the worse for wear at King's hands, Creed busted out an NES Power Glove and landed a Shoryuken uppercut that exploded in a shower of sparks, knocking his burly foe flat on his back. The moment quickly went viral, and Creed's team would eventually triumph, emerging as the AEW World Trios Champions.

Creed is no stranger to video games; during his run with WWE, he ran the Up Up Down Down YouTube channel, where he competed with fellow performers in a wide variety of games. Wrestling and video games have formed a symbiotic relationship over the years, with top performers like Kenny Omega referencing games like Street Fighter and Final Fantasy 7 for his signature moves. Video games have also positively influenced professional wrestlers, with top WWE star Roman Reigns saying it's a popular downtime activity with his fellow wrestlers and better than some of the "extracurricular" exploits of previous generations.

In another video game crossover, former WWE champion Cody Rhodes played Guile in the live-action Street Fighter movie, which was released last month, and he even cosplayed as the character at WWE SummerSlam. Sadly, the film wasn't a big box-office hit, making only $100.7 million worldwide during its run (via Box Office Mojo). In comparison, the other Capcom-based movie, Resident Evil, was far more successful, generating over $416 million worldwide and making it the highest-grossing Resident Evil movie of all time.

I knew Spider-Man: Brand New Day would make a ridiculous amount of money when it landed on this summer's 2026 movie schedule. What I didn't expect was to hear Sony's top movie executive making a serious case for Tom Holland's latest superhero adventure to earn a Best Picture Oscar nomination. But here we are, and apparently, the studio is prepared to put some real effort into making it happen.

Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group chairman and CEO Tom Rothman recently spoke with Variety about the movie's extraordinary success and why he believes it deserves Academy voters' consideration. With Brand New Day earning roughly $2.5 billion worldwide and breaking the domestic box office record, Rothman thinks there's something special about how audiences connected with Peter Parker's story. He explained:

The reason it did as much business as it did is not because it's a superhero movie, it's because it's a super person movie.

I actually get what he's saying. While I enjoyed the action in Brand New Day, what stuck with me was how much of the movie focused on Peter's loneliness after the events of No Way Home. Here's a guy who can swing between skyscrapers and take down some of Marvel's most dangerous villains, but he can't get the people he loves to remember who he is. That's a pretty miserable situation, even by Peter Parker standards.

Audiences clearly responded as well. The film received overwhelmingly positive reviews. It also became the highest-grossing movie in North American box office history, an accomplishment I imagine Sony will mention quite a bit over the next few months. But does all that mean it deserves an Oscar nomination?

Rothman certainly thinks so. When asked whether or not a strong box office means Brand New Day should be a Best Picture contender, he responded:

Once upon a time there were five best picture nominations, and then it was expanded to ten, to try to make room, I think, for quality commercial filmmaking… we’re biased, but we think [it should be nominated] so. We hope people will think about it.

Sony is backing up those comments with an actual campaign. According to Deadline, the studio has hired awards consultants and is planning special screenings and filmmaker Q&As beginning ahead of Thanksgiving. There's also talk of a theatrical rerelease designed to put the movie back in front of audiences and Academy voters.

Of course, superhero movies have historically struggled to crack the Best Picture category. Black Panther earned a nomination in 2019, followed by Joker the next year, but neither won. Even Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight missed a Best Picture nomination, despite earning eight Oscar nods and winning two.

As for Spider-Man, the character, he hasn't exactly been an Academy favorite. Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2 won Best Visual Effects in 2005, while Into the Spider-Verse took home Best Animated Feature in 2019. Although no movie starring the web-slinger has ever competed for Best Picture.

Still, I can understand Rothman's reasoning. Director Destin Daniel Cretton made a movie that made room for surprisingly intimate character moments, even amid all the enormous superhero spectacle. CinemaBlend's Jerrica Tisdale previously explained why that balance made the movie work so well, and I think it's a fair argument. Whether Academy voters agree is another matter entirely.

The nominations for the 99th Academy Awards will be announced Jan. 21, 2027, and Brand New Day will have some stiff competition. After watching what Sony and Marvel accomplished with Peter Parker this summer, I'm certainly not going to dismiss the idea outright. Besides, if anybody deserves a little recognition after everything he's been through, it's Peter Parker. The poor guy could use a win.

Most Spider-Man movies, past and present, are available to stream with your Disney+ subscription.

#3560. Billy Crystal Answers the Proust Questionnaire

Which historical figure do you most identify with?

My wife, Janice. Fearless, smart, optimistic, hilarious, loving…adored by all.

What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?

Self-doubt. Wait, now I’m not sure of the answer. Was that okay? Can we come back to that one?

What is the trait you most deplore in others?

From my dressing room to backstage—standing alone in the dark, a deep breath, and then feeling it’s time and walking out into the light.

What do you consider the most overrated virtue?

What do you dislike most about your appearance?

I’d rather not say, and thank you for your attention to this matter!

Which words or phrases do you most overuse?

“Sorry, I didn’t see your text till now.”

That my father died when I was 15 and never got to see my family, my career, and the man I think I am.

What or who is the greatest love of your life?

In the hospital waiting room, when my girls were born, and the doctor said everyone was fine.

Which talent would you most like to have?

If you could change one thing about yourself, what would it be?

I’d stop worrying about everyone all the time.

If you could change one thing about your family, what would it be?

That they’d finally understand why I worry about everyone all the time

What do you consider your greatest achievement?

We raised two fantastic daughters who became good, hard-working, honest people and great spouses and mothers in the middle of this business.

If you were to die and come back as a person or thing, what do you think it would be?

If you could choose what to come back as, what would it be?

I lost them all, so I’d have to say my memory.

What do you regard as the lowest depth of misery?

Love, empathy, loyalty, a sense of humor, and a handful of quarters for the parking meters.

Hemingway, David Sedaris, Neil Simon, Herb Gardner, Arthur Miller, Victor Hugo.

Santiago, the fisherman in The Old Man and the Sea.

Picasso, Muhammad Ali, Mickey Mantle, Buster Keaton, Sid Caesar, Mel Brooks, JFK, Alan Shepard—and Jim Redmond, a father who ran out of the stands at the ’92 Olympics to help his son, Derek, who had torn a hamstring in his race and was struggling to stand up and continue. They held onto each other and crossed the finish line together. Perfect.

Holding Janice’s hand. Ready, not frightened, satisfied, and with a smile and a goodbye to my family. And if there’s a laugh, that’s the last thing I hear? That would be great.

#3559. The Hunger Games Officially Changes Genres With a Near-Perfect New Movie

It’s also one of the best films in the franchise

The Hunger Games has never been afraid to put its young characters through the wringer. Despite being one of the most successful book and film franchises in history, the source material always stays true to its bleak premise: this is a story where teen bodies are used to keep the public under control.

More than a decade after the first film debuted, the franchise remains as relevant as ever, especially as our real world continues to look more and more like the dystopian nation of Panem. In 2023, we got a movie, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, exploring the backstory of the franchise’s main villain, President Snow. Francis Lawrence’s Sunrise on the Reaping, his fifth Hunger Games movie, is a direct sequel to that story, and while it’s still YA, he and his team push the boundaries of what we can expect from the genre. The result is an incredibly entertaining blockbuster with the feel of a bleak, existential horror movie.

Sunrise on the Reaping follows 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), a charming and hard-working boy from District 12, the poorest district in Panem. To make ends meet and take care of his mom and little brother, he illegally distills and sells moonshine. He spends his free time with his girlfriend, Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), even though her family doesn’t approve of him.

The story picks up on Reaping Day. This year is special, marking the 50th annual Hunger Games. To celebrate, the Capitol is demanding four tributes per district instead of two. After a boy’s name is called out and he runs off in fear, the reaping devolves into chaos. The boy gets shot, and Haymitch gets involved, trying to protect Lenore Dove from some Peacekeepers. To keep the show going and capture footage the Capitol can air, Haymitch is selected as the substitute tribute, and his journey begins.

If this all feels familiar, it should. While the Capitol comes off as particularly calculating, with the film paying close attention to how Snow (Ralph Fiennes) and his associates doctor footage for their own ends, Lawrence still follows the formula established by the original films. It isn’t until kids start dying before the Games begin that you realize Sunrise on the Reaping is doing something else. This is not a survival story; we all know where Haymitch ends up. This is a story about watching a character lose everything they care about.

While The Hunger Games movies always feature amazing actors, the cast for Sunrise on the Reaping is almost comically stacked. Fiennes brings his particular brand of menace to Coriolanus Snow, a character who develops a fixation on Haymitch. Glenn Close plays Drusilla Sickle, a Capitol escort sent to accompany the District 12 tributes (twist: she hates her job and the kids). Jesse Plemons takes over Plutarch Heavensbee from the late Philip Seymour Hoffman, playing him as aloof but quietly committed as he juggles making the show the Capitol wants and keeping Snow happy, all while fostering a rebellion among the tributes. At the center of it all is Zada, featured in almost every scene as he communicates an escalating sense of doom, loss, and despair.

Panem also gets a ’70s-style makeover. The Capitol is pushed decades into the past without losing its futuristic sheen, landing somewhere close to The Jetsons (complimentary). The best set is saved for what matters: the arena. It’s an open green field, lush and full of color, clear rivers, and adorable bunnies and deer. It’s a trick, though. The water is poisonous, and the animals are under the Capitol’s control. One tribute is killed by a swarm of squirrels. Another is impaled through the throat by a bird with a long, needle-thin beak. Haymitch’s plan to enter the arena and humiliate the Capitol on live TV is stymied at every turn, and Snow punishes him by making sure Haymitch gets a front seat to his friends’ deaths, one by one.

Sunrise on the Reaping is a tragedy. If you’ve seen the previous films, you know that Haymitch is an alcoholic from District 12, reviled by his community, and that it takes him meeting Katniss and forming a friendship with her for him to finally thaw. Sunrise on the Reaping effectively fills in the blanks of his character. At times, I found myself thinking, “There’s no way this could get worse,” but the film consistently proves me wrong.

It’s no secret that Sunrise on the Reaping also features the return of Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson. It’s a sweet moment for fans, but also the weakest part of the film, muddling an otherwise thoughtful and engaging blockbuster with bad wigs and nostalgia. The cameos feel like reassurance that there’s a light at the end of the tunnel for Haymitch, undercutting the dread that Lawrence was so committed to building in the first place.

Still, Sunrise on the Reaping is the most depressing Hunger Games movie yet; Katniss and Peeta had it easy. And while it has the franchise’s blockbuster magic, it adds a welcome dose of dread and tragic inevitability, easily elevating it to one of the series’ best movies.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premieres in theaters Nov. 20

Kelly Clarkson never fails to entertain or make me emotional on The Voice. I enjoy seeing her bring out the heartfelt words of encouragement, maybe even more than I enjoy watching her attempt to steal country singers from Riley Green. (But only slightly.) She never shies away from tearing up, or channeling what she learned from her American Idol days, which is what she used to give advice to contestants whenever The Voice goes live.

Something about the way the singer digs deep into the emotions really hits home. The Clarkson's advice may be a little "dark" as she reminds contestants to live in every moment, but there’s also something beautifully human about it. Clarkson is possibly influenced by the passing of her ex-husband Brandon Blackstock when she reminds her team that life is short. She shares with People ahead of The Voice’s live shows in early November what she tells contestants:

I know this sounds dark and I don’t mean it to. I mean it to sound so beautiful and in the moment and present, but you just don’t know how long you have on this planet. We’re artists, enjoy the moment. You might mess up and that’s OK, as long as people want to watch people being incredible at what they do.

Clarkson knows exactly what they’re experiencing. Not only did she go through a similar competition on American Idol, but she often performs live at concerts, events, and even during her former show’s “Kellyoke” segments. This is part of the reason her talk show was so popular, even winning multiple daytime Emmys for outstanding series.

While Clarkson has definitely upped her zany antics, including trying to give a contestant her hair, she’s also continues to bring the emotions. There’s always at least one singer who brings Clarkson (and the rest of us) to tears, and it all has to do with her appreciation for experiencing every moment. That’s exactly what she wants her team to know, even if it makes her sound like a mom:

I didn’t want them to be so nervous. It sounds really cheesy but really being present in the moment like, ‘Hey this is a really special thing that you’re getting to do right now. Really take that in.’ I’m such a mom.

As a mom of two, this has likely impacted her outlook on competition, especially when it comes to younger contestants like 13-year-old Brianna Cameron. Though who didn't share a tear during "Inseparable"? However, it’s not all emotional on The Voice as Clarkson reminds us yet again why she may just be the funniest Coach.... even if this season gave her some humorous competition. Whether it’s engaging in some smack talk with her fellow coaches or upping the goofy hijinks, it’s obvious she’s having a good time.

Season 30 has been a blast, and it’s largely due to the four coaches, which includes Adam Levine and newbie coaches Queen Latifah and Riley Green. However, while I’ve enjoyed the zany zingers and even the duck blind prank, it’s the emotional moments and performances that seem to land a little harder.

You can watch new episodes of The Voice every Monday on NBC and the next day with a Peacock subscription. The season is quickly winding down with the finale just around the corner on December 14.

#3556. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond

It looks like Robert Pattinson is trading in his Batmobile for an Aston Martin. After a highly scrutinized and lengthy audition process involving some of Hollywood’s most sought-after leading men, it was the Batman star who emerged at the eleventh hour to nab the role of MI6 agent James Bond.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” said Pattinson in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Created by Ian Fleming for his 1953 novel Casino Royale, James Bond, the British intelligence officer who lends his immense talents to MI6, is one of the most recognizable characters in the modern world. Figuring prominently in 12 of Fleming’s novels and two collections of short stories, Bond is both tall, dark, and handsome and calm, cool, and collected—the platonic ideal of a world-class spy. Bond leapt from page to screen in 1962 with the Eon-produced Dr. No, spawning one of the biggest media franchises in history. Since its inception, the 27 Bond films have grossed more than $7 billion dollars worldwide.

Pattinson follows in the suave footsteps of Daniel Craig, who played James Bond for five films, from 2006’s Casino Royale until 2021’s No Time to Die where (spoiler alert) Craig’s 007 dies while protecting the world from a global terrorist organization. Around No Time to Die, there was another shake up in Bond ownership when Amazon acquired Bond’s parent studio, MGM, in an $8.5 billion deal. Barbara Broccoli—whose father, Eon founder Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli, produced the first Bond film—and her half brother, Michael G. Wilson, held the rights to the franchise for almost 30 years, and pledged to work with Amazon. However, in February 2025, Broccoli and Wilson announced that they’d be stepping back from the franchise and ceding complete creative control to Amazon MGM. At the Oscars a month later, the Broccoli family was honored with a bizarre musical tribute to James Bond, starring Margaret Qualley, Doja Cat, and Lisa, unofficially ushering in a new era in the Bond Cinematic Universe.

Although a new era of Bond loomed, Amazon MGM had one major problem: They needed a new Bond. Ahead of No Time to Die, Craig had announced that he was stepping away from the franchise, leaving the producers with a 007-sized hole to fill. Before she stepped away, Broccoli insinuated that this new era of Bond was looking for a younger actor, in their 30s, to take over the reins from Craig, who was 51 when he retired from MI6.

Technically, they landed on someone slightly outside their preferred age range; Pattinson is 40 years old. Just don’t tell him that. During Vanity Fair’s lie detector test with Jennifer Lawrence while promoting their film Die My Love, Pattinson insisted he was from a different generation. I am Gen Z,” he said to Lawrence. “I am.” Hey, you’re only as old as you feel. In the same video, Pattinson said he “likes taking jobs of younger actors,” which he managed to do with his Bond casting. Good for Pattinson.

Almost every leading man in Hollywood’s name came up as a potential predecessor to Craig—except for Pattinson, who the masses assumed was out of contention due to the fact that he locked into playing another beloved fictional character with massive IP: Batman. Pattinson’s take on the caped crusader in Matt Reeve’s The Batman (2022) was a major success, but several production delays on The Batman Part II, and a shakeup at Batman’s studio, DC—last week, it was announced that the co-CEOs of DC Productions, James Gunn and Peter Safran, were ousted from the studio—meant that there might be time in Pattinson’s schedule for some sexy espionage.

Still, it was far from a done deal that Pattinson would land 007. In recent years, some fans have advocated for a twist on the classic Bond formula. Lashana Lynch made history as Nomi, the first Black person to ever to hold the 007 moniker, in No Time to Die. But Nomi is not James Bond. There was a seemingly endless period when the world was convinced that Idris Elba—arguably the most tall, dark, and handsome man to ever exist—would take on the mantle at some point, but it wasn’t meant to be. Now, at 53, Elba has seemingly aged out of the role. (For the record, Elba thought the next Bond should be a woman.) Elba wasn’t the only name bandied about in recent years. It was reported in 2024 that Aaron Taylor-Johnson was close to signing a contract to take over the role, but those reports were never confirmed.

Although a favorite at the beginning, Jacob Elordi reportedly didn’t screen test for the role. Riz Ahmed made an Emmy-nominated television show, Bait, inspired by the idea of a British Pakistani actor getting cast as Bond. Other actors rumored to be in the mix over the course of the process include, but are not limited to, Tom Francis, Harris Dickinson, and, apparently, Harry Styles. At the end of the day, five actors reportedly screen-tested for the role: Slow Horse’s Jack Lowden, One Night Only’s Callum Turner, Disclosure Day’s Josh O’Connor, Superman’s Nicholas Hoult, and Pattison. Hoult and Pattinson were the last names to emerge as contenders for the role, implying that the powers that be at Amazon MGM may not have been happy with the three options presented and sent a hail mary. When Puck reported that Pattinson was able to negotiate a three-picture deal rather than a four-picture deal despite commanding a much higher salary than the other options, it looked like the writing was on the wall that Pattinson would be the next Bond.

It also helps that Pattinson is having a career high at the moment, having starred in a handful of the most critically acclaimed and commercially successful films of 2026. He began the year by turning his controversial A24 comedy The Drama with Zendaya into a box-office success, generating $134 million worldwide on a reported budget of about $28 million. He then followed that up with a deliciously sniveling turn in Christopher Nolan’s epic The Odyssey, an Oscar front-runner that earned $1.8 billion at the box office. Then there’s Primetime, the Lance Oppenheim drama starring Pattinson as To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen. (Yes, in a way, Chris Hansen is now one degree from being James Bond. Let that sink in). Primetime hit big with $62 million globally on an $14.5 million budget, and is earning Pattinson leading-actor buzz. On top of it all, he’s still got Dune: Part Three with Denis Villeneuve coming down the pipeline in December.

Ultimately, the Twilight star was handpicked by the powers that be at Amazon MGM, including producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and director Denis Villeneuve, who is helming the next iteration of the series based on a script from screenwriter Steven Knight, with Tanya Lapointe executive producing. Given the fact that Pattinson is starring in Villeneuve’s highly-anticipated Dune: Part Three, it might not be that much of a surprise that the director chose Pattinson as his next Bond. “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” said Villeneuve in a statement. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

Pattinson enters a long lineage of spectacularly suave spies—some who lasted longer than others in Bond’s impeccably tailored suits. The first-ever James Bond was, of course, Sean Connery, who went on to star in six Bond films, including From Russia With Love (1963), Goldfinger (1964), and Diamonds Are Forever (1971). Connery was followed by George Lazenby, who starred in a single Bond film, On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969), before passing the reins back to Connery. The third Bond was Roger Moore, who took over for 1973’s Live and Let Die, and appeared in a total of seven Bond films, most notably The Spy Who Loved Me (1977) and Octopussy (1983).

After Moore came Timothy Dalton, who became 007 with 1987’s The Living Daylights, then threw in the towel after 1989’s License to Kill. Millennials will fondly remember the next Bond: Pierce Brosnan, who starred as the sexy spy in four films from 1995’s GoldenEye to 2002’s Die Another Day, until Craig took over in 2006.

Will Pattison’s Bond be more debonair like Brosnan, who told VF he was “eagerly” awaiting the Bond casting news, or brooding like Craig? Will he be remembered as a rightful heir to Connery’s throne, or will his Bond feel closer to Austin Powers in The Spy Who Shagged Me? In any case, let’s hope Pattinson prefers his martinis shaken not stirred. He’s going to be drinking a lot of them for the foreseeable future.

It’s hard to believe it’s been over 14 years since audiences first saw Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen volunteer as tribute for the 74th Hunger Games. While so much time has passed, that series of book-to-screen adaptations remains greatly loved by fans. Lawrence herself seems to have an appreciation for that time in her life as well even if it wasn’t always easy for her to control the craziness. Ahead of her return as Katniss, Lawrence shared a sweet throwback pic of herself with two of her key co-stars, and her caption is great.

Lawrence is set to play Katniss for the first time in over a decade in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which is set to hit the 2026 movie schedule in a matter of days. It would seem that the Oscar winner is feeling a bit nostalgic, as she recently took to her Instagram stories to share some classic pics, possibly from press tours from the early aughts. One particularly sweet photo shows Lawrence alongside Peeta Mellark actor Josh Hutcherson and Gale Hawthorne star Liam Hemsworth. Check out it below:

The mere sight of this lovely photo is enough to hit someone with a hearty helping of early 2010s nostalgia. I can still remember the sheer amount of buzz that surrounded the release of the first Hunger Games movie adapted from Suzanne Collins’ beloved book series. What we see in that picture are the smiling faces of three people in the midst of an amazing professional journey. Also, leave it to “J. Law” to choose such a cheeky caption for the photo and, let’s be real, the statement isn’t untrue either.

What I really want to know is when exactly this photo was taken. I mean, was this taken around the time the OG film in the young adult franchise came out or at a later date. Regardless, I appreciate Lawrence sharing such sweet mementos, and you can check out another post down below. This one features two black-and-white photos — one of the trio hanging out on what appears to be a bridge and another shot of them on a bed:

Jennifer Lawrence is practically revered for her role as Katniss at this point, as many still hold her performance in high regard, including others who’ve since joined the franchise. Earlier this year, Sunrise on the Reaping’s Maya Hawke praised Lawrence for her character’s impact on the action genre. Ironically, Lawrence explained years ago that she was scared to sign on for the movies, given such blockbusters can “make or break a career.” I think it’s safe to say that everything turned out fine, though.

Josh Hutcherson has also expressed warm feelings about the reception he’s received for his performance as Peeta, which has blown fans away. Though Hutcherson had been away from the franchise for some time, he admitted last fall that he felt a bit of FOMO over not being a part of the newer films. That has changed, however, as Hutcherson is reprising Peeta alongside Lawrence’s Katniss and Woody Harrelson’s (older) Haymitch Abernathy in the latest installment.

How exactly that aforementioned trio of actors factors into this prequel film is unclear at the moment. Nevertheless, I’m sure fans are just pleased that they’ll be returning in some kind of capacity. For now, though, I just find it lovely that Jennifer Lawrence is embracing her memories, and I hope she and the “girls” are able to somehow make some new ones down the road.

Check out The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping when it opens in theaters on November 20. In the meantime, stream the original four films now with a Peacock subscription, or check them out for free on Tubi.

#3554. Zendaya “Felt Overwhelmed” on the Set of ‘The Odyssey.’ Luckily, Tom Holland Came to Support Her

On the set of The Odyssey, in which Zendaya plays the goddess Athena, there were some particularly challenging days, as the actor recalled during a recent special screening attended by the cast at Los Angeles’s Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. While filming certain scenes—especially those with a crowd of extras—the 30-year-old actor felt “incredibly nervous,” she said.

How did she manage to keep the situation under control? Thank her husband, Tom Holland, whom Zendaya says went to set that day to cheer her up. Spider-Man: Brand New Day star Holland also appears in The Odyssey as Telemachus, son of Odysseus and Penelope. And although he wasn’t scheduled to work at that particular moment, he showed up anyway to support his wife.

Matt Damon’s Odysseus consults with Zendaya’s Athena in The Odyssey.

“I felt overwhelmed, to say the least,” Zendaya said at the screening, as reported by the Daily Mail, with the actor looking stunning in her cream-colored one-shoulder dress, pixie cut, and Christian Louboutin stilettos. “It was interesting because I was on a night shoot, and I remember I came in and I was like, This is like, a pinch-me moment…. I’m in front of these people who I’ve admired, but I’m just like, I don’t want to mess this up.”

While she admitted that these emotions might have worked for her character, they were not so good for her state of mind: “I was incredibly nervous, which I guess is helpful for the scene, but there’s so many other background actors as well who are performing their hearts out—so many—stunt performers who are performing and giving the most beautiful performances.”

The turning point came when Holland stepped behind the scenes to encourage her. “It helped that Tom came to set that day, and he was, like, in the corner like, ‘You got this, you’re doing good.’” It was a team effort.

Zendaya and Holland are one of Hollywood’s most admired couples, not only for their discretion (they quietly married last August 4 in Surrey) but also for the care with which they address sensitive issues, such as mental health. Even in the cult series Euphoria, Zendaya’s character, Rue, grapples with psychological issues—in addition to addiction—as a way to raise public awareness and combat the stigma that often surrounds these kinds of situations.

#3553. My Favorite Sony Headphones Are Over $80 Off Right Now

One of the best headphone deals right now is for my favorite headphones: Sony's 1000X series has been around since 2016, with each new model improving on the previous iteration, the latest being the Sony WH-1000XM6, released in 2025. These are the best over-ear headphones I tested in 2025 (or ever, really). Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $378 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools.

The XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to aware mode (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

These headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

The XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $378, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

#3552. The Game Awards 2026 Nominees Reveal: Here's How to Watch

The annual awards show will reveal its contenders just days before GTA 6 arrives

The Game Awards 2026 is fast approaching, and this year's award nominees are set to be announced on Tuesday, Nov. 17. The nominees will be revealed during a dedicated livestream — that just happens to be coming two days ahead of the year's most anticipated game, Grand Theft Auto 6.

Fans will be able to watch the TGAs Nomination Special on Tuesday via YouTube and Twitch. Host and executive producer Geoff Keighley will announce the games, studios, and talent nominated for this year's awards, which will include Game of the Year.

The Game Awards 2026 Nomination Special will be livestreamed on Tuesday, Nov. 17, starting at 9 a.m. PST/12 p.m. EST. In past years, Keighley has made the special pretty efficient; the event usually takes around 10 minutes. Nominees for Game of the Year are typically announced at the very end of the special.

Voting for fan-based awards will go live immediately after The Game Awards 2026 Nomination Special concludes.

Yes. According to The Game Awards' official website, games eligible for this year's main awards "must be made commercially available to customers on or before Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9 p.m. PT." Grand Theft Auto 6 will squeak in ahead of that; the game is officially being released on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

For the TGA's Players’ Voice category, games must ship on or before Nov. 30, 2026, organizers say. So if you're thinking about voting for GTA 6, you have ample time to spend with the game to make up your mind.

The Game Awards 2026 will be held on Thursday, Dec. 10. The show starts at 4:30 p.m. PST/7:30 p.m. EST, including the traditional 30-minute pre-show.

This year's The Game Awards will stream on more platforms than ever, with Disney Plus, Live TV on PS5, and Roblox joining the long list of platforms on which to watch. The show will also be available on YouTube, Twitch, Steam, TikTok Live, X, Kick, Facebook, and Instagram Live. In China, the show will be available on more than 20 platforms, including Baidu, Bilibili, Douyin, DouYu, Huya, WeChat, Weibo and Xiaohongshu. Additional partners include CHZZK and SOOP in South Korea; NicoNico in Japan; Vidio in Indonesia; Now TV in Hong Kong; mewatch in Singapore; and BIGO LIVE and Likee across Southeast Asia.

#3551. This Bose Portable Bluetooth Speaker Is 33% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

Some spoilers for The Nights Before Christmas can be found in this piece.

Hallmark is no stranger to holiday time-loop movies — the 2023 time-loop film Round and Round was my absolute favorite that year — so they definitely know how to write an effective one. Just like Hallmark Christmas movies follow a perfect movie formula, time-loop flicks also have a tried-and-true formula. A character who is unhappy in life encounters some kind of magical being or object that sets up the time loop, which they’ll ultimately spend the rest of the film trying desperately to break the curse.

Such core elements are so ingrained in the genre that it can be hard to reinvent the time-loop wheel, but by some miracle, Hallmark managed to do just that. And it totally worked!

The Nights Before Christmas premiered on the 2026 TV schedule this weekend and instantly became one of my favorite Hallmark Christmas movies of 2026. A fun yuletide flick, it follows Marty (Tyler Hynes), who is stuck reliving Christmas Eve over and over again after making a holiday wish to have more time to pursue his interests and hobbies. Marty takes full advantage of the gift of time, using it to meet people and master all his hobbies, and he seems content to keep living the same day on repeat.

Well, that is, until he meets Chloe (Laci J. Mailey), whom he feels an instant connection with. As Marty continues to repeat Christmas Eve with Chloe, he starts to wonder what his life would be like if he made it to Christmas morning.

Unlike other time-loop films, The Nights Before Christmas doesn’t start on day one of Marty’s loop. Instead, we meet Marty in one of the hundreds, if not thousands, of Christmas Eves he’s managed to live through. This is in immediate deviation from the genre that has made finding out you're in a time loop and freaking out about it one of the main features of a character’s arc. He’s also not freaked out or bothered by the sudden change in how time progresses; if anything, he welcomes and loves it.

The realization that this wasn’t going to be a day-one time loop was one that shocked me as soon as it happened, but I was totally on board with it. Admittedly, I’m not the biggest fan of the genre, so getting to watch Marty exist in the loop and be happy with his new, repetitive life was a much-needed and refreshing change to the otherwise predictable genre.

My Favorite Hallmark Christmas Movie Is Getting A Sequel, And I Can’t Wait

The film continues to reinvent the wheel as it progresses. For starters, almost every time Marty explains to Chloe that he’s stuck in a time loop, she believes him. This is unheard of with these types of films, as most of the time the stuck character has to jump through extravagant hoops to get anyone to believe and help them. Perhaps it helps that Marty isn’t asking for Chloe’s help in getting unstuck or advice on how to survive said time loop; he simply wants to spend time with her.

TNBC also finds fun ways to show the same day over and over again without long, drawn-out scenes. There’s a particularly fun sequence towards the end of the film where Marty is shown to be an excellent driver in a terrible snowstorm, despite having previously claimed to hate driving. It’s then revealed that this isn’t the first time he’s driven in the terrible storm and that the previous attempts have ended in disaster.

In its final act, the holiday film also manages to reinvent the way the time loop is resolved. All too often in these types of movies, the main characters must come to some great epiphany in order to put a stop to the loop and revert to the real timeline. This usually involves searching inward and changing something about themselves, but that’s not what happens in Nights Before Christmas. Instead, Marty discovers that he wasn’t put in the time loop to help himself, but rather he was put there to help Chloe get the Christmas she’s come to love and expect: a day with her parents. Needless to say, a narrative like this is quite refreshing in this genre.

So, if you’re a fan of time loops and Christmas, then The Nights Before Christmas needs to go to the top of your holiday watch list. The film can be streamed now with an active Hallmark+ subscription, or viewers can catch it airing on Hallmark again on Friday, November 20th at 10 PM, after the latest Countdown to Christmas lineup premiere.

Danielle Bruncati is a writer and pop culture enthusiast from Southern California. She earned a Master of Fine Arts degree in Television Writing and Producing from a top film school. Her goal is to one day be the writer on a show/movie covered by Cinemablend, but for now, she's excited to be a Freelance Writer here.

Danielle watches just about everything, but her favorite shows and movies often land in the YA and romantic comedy spaces. When she's not writing, she can be found wandering around Disneyland or hanging out with her laughter-hating corgi.

#3549. Glenn Close Gets Teary-Eyed as She Finally Gets Her Oscar at the Governors Awards

The day before the Governors Awards, a studio executive who had attended the past few years told me that she often found herself crying at the star-studded gala. The annual awards ceremony, held by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, is often an emotional event, with honorary Oscar statuettes bestowed on influential figures in the film industry. A tribute to Michael J. Fox in 2022 and a posthumous honor for Quincy Jones in 2024 left many guests misty-eyed.

At Sunday’s gala, that teary-eyed trend continued when Glenn Close finally got to hold her own Oscar, after eight nominations without a win. Others got emotional when Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, the independent producers from Killer Films, were honored for their tireless work making boundary-pushing and challenging movies. And when Floyd Norman, the 91-year-old artist who was the first Black animator to join Walt Disney Animation Studios, thanked his wife and five children, the crowd cheered along with him. Even though honoree Ridley Scott couldn’t attend, he dedicated his award to his late brother Tony Scott in a video message. “It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand,” said Matt Damon in his remarks for Scott, who has been nominated for four Oscars but has never won competitively.

The presentation of honorary Oscars is often a way to correct Academy Award history, recognizing those who have been overlooked but deserve to be honored for their lifetime of dedication to storytelling and film. The Governors Awards ceremony is also a major stop on the Oscar season campaign trail, with a room packed full of stars and filmmakers from the year’s contenders.

This year that meant a surprising number of couple contenders, including Monica Barbaro and Andrew Garfield (who both star in Artificial), Carrie Coon and Tracy Letts (The Liberation), and Zendaya and Tom Holland. Though Zendaya and Holland arrived together and walked through the Ray Dolby Ballroom as a pair, they actually sat at different tables—Zendaya at the Dune table, with Timothée Chalamet and director Denis Villeneuve, and Holland at the Odyssey table, with director Christopher Nolan. Chalamet also made a date night out of the event, bringing Kylie Jenner with him.

The room held a mix of A-list Hollywood stars, like Tom Cruise (in support of Digger), Julianne Moore (The Debut), and Charlize Theron (The Odyssey), and breakout filmmakers of the year, like Obsession’s Curry Barker, La Bola Negra’s Los Javis, and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman.

Another breakout of the season, La Bola Negra star Guitarricadelafuente, has been busy promoting the film as both an actor and a musician, having written the original song “La Nieve.” I wondered if he was exhausted from doing double duty. “I’m not tired,” he said with a smile, raving that he had enjoyed meeting many of the other songwriters in the race this year.

All four of the presenters who handed the Oscars to the honorees are also in the Oscar race this year. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star Mahershala Ali honored Norman; Wild Horse Nine star John Malkovich honored his Dangerous Liaisons costar Close; Julianne Moore, teaming up with Todd Haynes, honored Vachon and Koffler; and Damon, the star of The Odyssey, honored Scott.

As Close took the stage to accept the award from Malkovich, she wiped tears away from her eyes. The star of films including Fatal Attraction, 101 Dalmatians, The Wife, Albert Nobbs, and The Big Chill spoke about being raised in a religious cult and how, in her childhood, animated films were her only escape. She also spoke about being nominated for eight Oscars over her career, insisting that it didn’t phase her not to emerge victorious. “As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not,” she says. “I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room.”

She wrapped up her speech with a strong statement against AI. “The craft of acting and of great storytelling has never been more vital to the existence of our fragile, violent, but capable-of-transcendence species,” she said. “We are not machines. We are flawed. Our imperfections are our salvation.”

Vachon and Koffler have been making indie films through Killer Films since 1995, championing movies like Far From Heaven, Boys Don’t Cry, Kids, Carol, and Still Alice (which won Moore her Academy Award for lead actress). They dedicated their awards to the many people they’d worked with over the years, some of whom were in the room. “We have walked into propellers with you and what has resulted is usually a piece of work that has touched somebody. Sometimes it’s seen by millions of people and sometimes it’s seen by tens of people,” said Vachon. “But our movies came to life and made it to the screen because writers and directors trusted us with their stories and actors knew we were creating an environment that enabled them to give their best performance.”

Many of the honorees spoke about the mentors and industry giants who had helped them along the way. Close said she’d promised her World According to Garp director, George Roy Hill, that she’d thank him if she ever won an Oscar. “I never got the chance to thank the man who put me in my first movie. Now I can,” she said, holding her statuette up high. Scott, the director whose prolific career output includes Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, Alien, Blade Runner, and The Martian, told a story in his video message about making his brother star in his very first project, the 1965 short film Boy and Bicycle. “I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony,” Scott said of his brother, who died in 2012. “His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

#3548. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

Johnny Depp is officially back in Hollywood, at least as far as his career is concerned. His 2026 movie release, Ebenezer, just topped the domestic box office, marking his first major studio release in eight years. But while the actor is making his way back onto movie screens (even for lesser pay), he's apparently in no hurry to return to living in the United States. In fact, he's been spending most of his time somewhere that sounds an awful lot like a vacation destination.

The Pirates of the Caribbean star recently spoke with The Wall Street Journal about his childhood, his unlikely introduction to acting and where he calls home these days. I knew Depp owned an island in the Bahamas, but I hadn't realized just how much time he actually spends there. According to the 63-year-old actor:

Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody's pointing a camera at me or staring.

I suppose having your own island makes avoiding the paparazzi considerably easier. And considering how much attention Depp's personal life has received over the years, I can understand why he'd want somewhere he can go about his day without somebody pointing a camera at him.

Yet what I found particularly interesting was how the Oscar nominee described the property itself. Depp purchased Little Hall's Pond Cay, a 45-acre island in the Bahamas, in 2004 for a reported $3.6 million. And while I pictured some enormous Caribbean mansion, his description of the place sounds surprisingly modest. He continued:

I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me.

A wooden house, a yurt and somewhere to paint. Not exactly what I would have pictured for the man who spent years playing one of Disney's most recognizable characters, but I can appreciate the appeal.

Depp also told the publication that he enjoys reading and playing guitar in his music studio, which sounds about right for somebody who originally moved to Los Angeles hoping to make it as a musician.

Forget Scrooge, Johnny Depp Will Soon Be Back On The Big Screen For What May Be His Scariest Role Ever

His current living situation is especially interesting considering how frequently his family moved when he was growing up. Depp recalled relocating approximately 40 times during his childhood, particularly after his family moved from Kentucky to Florida. The constant changes made it difficult to settle in, and he described himself as an outsider.

Music eventually became his escape. His mother gave him an acoustic guitar when he was 12, and by 1983, Depp had moved to Los Angeles with his band, hoping to make a career out of playing music. Then he met Nicolas Cage.

According to Depp, the two became friends after Cage started attending his band's performances. Eventually, Cage suggested that he try acting and helped connect him with an agent. That led to his film debut in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street, followed by the career that made him one of Hollywood's biggest stars.

Of course, his relationship with Hollywood became considerably more complicated in recent years. Depp stepped away from major American studio productions amid legal battles with his ex-wife, Amber Heard, including their highly publicized 2022 defamation trial. He continued working internationally, appearing in the French film Jeanne du Barry and directing Modi: Three Days on the Wing of Madness.

Now, he's back with Ti West's Ebenezer, which opened Nov. 13 and earned an estimated $19 million domestically during its first weekend. But does the box-office win signal a larger Hollywood comeback? Only time will tell, but Depp has another major American release on the horizon: Day Drinker, a thriller co-starring Penélope Cruz, arriving on the 2027 movie schedule. Still, his latest comments suggest returning to American movies doesn't necessarily mean returning to a US address.

The '80s heartthrob has owned his Bahamian retreat for more than two decades, so this isn't some sudden relocation following his Hollywood troubles. But hearing him describe how much time he spends there gives a better idea of what his life looks like these days. After years of playing Jack Sparrow, I suppose it's fitting that Johnny Depp found a little peace on an island of his own.

Ebenezer is now playing in theaters, so check your local listings for showtimes. If you want to revisit Depp's iconic portrayal of Captain Jack, all the Pirates of the Caribbean films stream with a Disney+ subscription.
