#3531. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3530. Timothée Chalamet Came Over for Lunch—and a Cover Story

The history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

On more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”

Timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the New York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s new film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron ­Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

In case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived New Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.

Fashion Editor: Taylor McNeill. Hair and grooming products by Augustinus Bader. Grooming by Jamie Taylor. Produced on location by Object & Animal and Truenorth. For details, go to VF.com/credits.

#3529. Marvel's Vision Was Originally Intended As A Revival Of A Forgotten Superhero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Since his introduction in 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," the Vision (Paul Bettany) has become one of the most enduring Marvel Cinematic Universe characters. Not even getting his vibranium head crushed by Thanos (Josh Brolin) back in "Avengers: Infinity War" stopped him from returning in the TV series "WandaVision" — in which Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) conjures the life she wanted with Vision — and "VisionQuest," which revisits Vision's relationship with Ultron (James Spader), his "father."

Created by Roy Thomas and John Buscema, Vision debuted in 1968's "The Avengers" issue #57. Unlike in the MCU, where Ultron creates Vision's "synthezoid" body for himself before the Avengers steal it, comic Ultron (then known as Ultron-5) created Vision as a conscious being to lure the Avengers to their doom. Vision then turned against his creator, and the following issue #58 saw him inaugurated as an Avenger.

But Vision as we know him almost didn't exist. Thomas is a fan of the "Golden Age of Comics," aka the earliest period of superhero comics in the 1940s. Back then, Marvel was called Timely Comics, and its superhero stable included Aarkus, an interdimensional being named The Vision. Created in 1940 by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby (the same year that they created Captain America), the Vision debuted in "Marvel Mystery" #13. Summoned to Earth by scientist Enoch Mason, Aarkus hails from a supernatural dimension called "Smokeworld."

Originally, Thomas wanted to bring back this Vision as an Avenger, as Stan Lee and Kirby had brought back Captain America in "Avengers" #4. But Lee (without giving a reason) insisted on an android hero instead, so Thomas and Buscema created a new Vision in the image of the 1940s one. Aarkus has made occasional reappearances, but he definitely sits in the shadow of the later Vision.

Roy Thomas, who wrote "The Avengers" from issue #35 through #104, sometimes felt like he was playing in the minor leagues. Speaking to Yahoo in 2015, Thomas recounted: "Stan [Lee] kept taking Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor away from the Avengers. Every few months I would request to bring them back to the fold. I would say, 'You left me with a bunch of losers here.'"

When looking for a new Avenger, Thomas wanted to revive the Golden Age Vision because "[he] didn't like to create new characters for Marvel, because [he] wouldn't own them."

Vision's origin honored Lee's request to make the new Avenger an android, but Thomas and John Buscema's Vision still looks a lot like Aarkus. They share a mostly green color scheme, a high collar cape, a bald head, etc. Vision's intangibility powers also evoke Aarkus appearing and disappearing in plumes of smoke. There are some different details, granted. Vision has a "solar gem" on his forehead (which Thomas credits to Buscema, and which the MCU tweaked into one of the Infinity Stones), as well as red skin (unlike Aarkus' pale green).

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in 2015, Thomas surmised that Lee wasn't totally satisfied with the Vision, noting he disliked the hero's red color ("Red's not a good color!") and the "Vision" name. "It seems a little wimpy, but I felt Vision — it really means like a ghost or a mirage or an image," Thomas explained.

Nonetheless, history shows Vision's creation came with a huge ripple effect, reshaping "The Avengers" forever. Many of the book's core storylines go back to Vision, like his romance with the Scarlet Witch or Ultron's persistent efforts to destroy the Avengers, his son included.

Ultron debuted only a few issues before Vision, in "Avengers" #54. Issue #57 saw Vision seemingly destroy his creator, while issue #58 revealed the Avenger Hank Pym/Ant-Man had created Ultron, leading to the robot rebelling and erasing his creator's memory. Roy Thomas told Yahoo, "I knew right away [Ultron] is a character you would bring back." So he did when, in "Avengers" #66, subliminal programming inside Vision makes him restore Ultron in a new adamantium body. As for Vision and the Scarlet Witch, Thomas told Syfy in 2022 that he paired them because Vision didn't have a solo title, so Thomas had sole control over Vision's story.

If Aarkus the Vision had become an Avenger, it's plausible he'd have filled a superficially similar role on the team. Perhaps he and Wanda would've even ended up together. But he'd lack the connection to Ultron, which would diminish the villain.

In a foreword to 2015's "Avengers: Rage of Ultron," former "Avengers" writer Kurt Busiek notes the Ultron-Vision thread running through "Avengers" is a family saga. The family theme also heightens the contradictions that make Ultron more than just a killer robot. He's literally inhuman, yet he behaves more like an angry and erratic child than a cold machine, closer to Frankenstein's Creature than Hal 9000.

This makes Thomas and John Buscema creating Vision, instead of resurrecting Aarkus, a lynchpin moment of entertainment history in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Stan Lee, Thomas, and Buscema, when pumping out cheaply-printed "Avengers" comics in the 1960s and '70s, could've hardly predicted Vision would be a major character in the biggest blockbuster property ever. Nor that an entire TV series would rest on Vision and Wanda's romance, and then another on Vision and Ultron's antagonistic bond.

Rick Devens has simple advice for those who want to be on reality television, and for anyone who wants to be on the best reality shows, I'd listen up. Apparently the key to getting in the position to win Big Brother, or make wild moves on Survivor, is to be bold... even if you look foolish.

While we've seen people win Big Brother and Survivor by playing the middle, the most memorable winners and players are the ones who make the big moves. Other reality stars may suggest being chill, but not Devens. He told The Observer the key to his moves is this:

I think that's some universal advice most reality stars would give, which is why they were put on TV to begin with. Casting directors don't seek out people who will strive to worry about every move that's on camera, what could go wrong, or make rash decisions.

Rick Devens just won Big Brother, so he's a great person to ask this question. Not many people get the chance to play on both BB and Survivor, so those should continue to listen when it comes to why it's important to be fearless. As he continued:

You’re going to handicap yourself. You’re going to keep yourself from doing amazing things and having the most fun. Just go for it. Be fearless.

All this to say, not every person on reality television is Rick Devens. He's speaking with the bias of someone who was put on Survivor initially and welcomed back because of how he played. It's that same fearlessness that got him on Big Brother, hoping that "Chaos Devens" would be activated.

There's been some debate of whether Devens played as fast and loose on BB as he did on Survivor. Coming in the game with built-in allies in Dee Valladares and Angela Murray, as well as being voted to receive powers, certainly allowed him some freedom to make moves that other Houseguests weren't afforded. I would imagine that if any of those other Houseguests had been given those big of powers, they would've also jumped on the opportunity.

Rick Devens and Big Brother's producers, for that matter, would argue he and the icons had the biggest targets on their backs going into the game. The advantages allowed them to "even the odds" and prevent being targeted from the jump and being sent out of the game immediately. Neither had pointed out that former winner Rachel Reilly played in the previous season with only one week of safety as an advantage, but I digress.

In any case, Rick and the Icons playing Big Brother again resulted in big ratings for the series and a two-season renewal. Bringing in the viewers will also work a lot toward getting someone back on reality television, so I'm just waiting to see if we'll see him again if Season 30 of BB does end up being an all-star season. In the meantime, I'll enjoy all his previous reality TV appearances on Paramount+.

#3527. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3526. After Gilligan's Island, Jim Backus And Alan Hale Jr. Reunited On A Legendary Western Series

"Gilligan's Island" might have been a silly slapstick sitcom, but it remains beloved even almost 60 years after it went off the air. Of course, after the third and final season, the castaways managed to keep themselves in the public consciousness via a syndication deal, two animated "Gilligan's Island" spin-offs, and three TV movies — and that's to say nothing of the unofficial reunions.

Members of the "Gilligan's Island" cast re-teamed on numerous projects in the years after the show proper went off the air. In fact, Captain Jonas Grumby and Thurston Howell III actors Alan Hale Jr. and Jim Backus couldn't wait to get back on-set together. The pair reunited a couple years after the castaways bid viewers farewell, when they both appeared in one of the best classic Western series: "The Wild Wild West."

This legendary show famously combined the sci-fi, spy, and Western genres to create a unique experience, which ran for four seasons on the network that also hosted "Gilligan's Island," CBS. "The Wild Wild West" debuted in September 1965, the same month the castaways returned for their second season. By 1969, however, "Gilligan's Island" had been off the air for two years while "The Wild Wild West" was entering its fourth and final season (though it, too, would live on via TV movies and an infamous big screen reimagining). It was during this final run that Hale Jr. and Backus both appeared in the episode "The Night of the Sabatini Death."

"The Wild Wild West" debuted at a time when the sci-fi genre was already beginning to supercede the Western. It ultimately took until the mid-'70s for Old West adventures to fall out of favor completely (though, if you'd have asked Roger Ebert he would have said 2001's Ali Larter-led "American Outlaws" finally killed the Western for good). Before the decline of this once beloved genre began in earnest, however, Michael Garrison conceived of a series which he famously envisioned as "James Bond on horseback." But that was only part of the "Wild Wild West" formula.

The show, set in the post-Civil war era, followed Secret Service agents James West (Robert Conrad) and Artemus Gordon (Ross Martin), who thwarted all manner of threat to the United States using advanced technology. That added a sci-fi element to the show's melding of the Western and spy genres, making it a triple threat that immediately proved popular. By the time Alan Hale, Jr. and Jim Backus guested, the show was well-established as a small screen favorite, even while CBS was preparing to drop the axe.

"The Night of the Sabatini Death" begins with dying crime boss Johnny Sabatini (Ted de Corsia) meeting Jim West. It seems the sickly kingpin wants West to ensure his niece, Caroline (Sylvia Nolan), receives a gift he's leaving her. West then travels to Calliope, Missouri, alongside his new agent colleague (Ross Martin was missing from several Season 4 episodes) Ned Brown, who's played by Hale Jr. In Calliope, West meets mortician Fabian Swanson (Backus) who is dispatched halfway through the episode, becoming a "customer of his own establishment" as West puts it.

At the end of "The Night of the Sabatini Death" Alan Hale Jr.'s Ned Brown departs, telling James West he plans to "spend a vacation all alone on a desert island." The "Gilligan's Island" theme then plays, confirming this is, indeed, a nod to Hale's Skipper role (poor old Jim Backus doesn't get to do anything near as fun).

Interestingly enough, Hale Jr. and Backus' appearance in "The Night of the Sabatini Death" was far from the only link between "Gilligan's Island" and "The Wild Wild West." Dawn Wells, who'd played Mary Ann Summers on the CBS sitcom also appeared on "The Wild Wild West" the year prior to her former co-stars. The actress guest starred in the 1968 episode "The Night of the Headless Woman," playing Betsy Jeffers, daughter of Richard Anderson's Commissioner James Jeffers. It was a brief appearance, but it meant she beat her "Gilligan's Island' colleagues to the series.

What's more, "The Wild Wild West" was one of many shows to make use of "Gilligan's Island" sets, most notably the lagoon which had been built on the CBS Studios backlot. "Gilligan's Island" also shared this set with "Gunsmoke," the show which ultimately forced the sitcom off the air. But it also came in handy for the adventures of James West and Artemus Gordon.

Sadly, those adventures came to an end shortly after Hale and Backus' guest appearances on the show. "The Wild Wild West" was ultimately canceled to appease a Congress eager to prove it was against violence in every form, including the small screen variety. Today, we can at least see Hale Jr. and Backus' "Wild Wild West" guest spots for free on Pluto TV.

#3525. Timothée Chalamet Talks ‘Dune 3,’ the Knicks, and His Hollywood Inspirations

Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good New Yorker entering someone’s apartment. On is just fine.

He’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he says—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano. He devours it in less than two minutes. We’ve met before, but definitely never hung out at home. I think he’s friends with Frank Ocean, so I throw on Channel Orange. I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants New York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

He’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

Late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he says, taking a big seat and resting his right arm along the back.

He glances down at the old issues of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 issue of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet says, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

It’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” New York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

In our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet says. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

Chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s new book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”

LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” says Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

You don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

The production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.)

Chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he says. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.)

“It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet says. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”

Production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet says. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

Part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he says “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

It was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet said goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows quickly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

“Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring new artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem says, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”

Safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” says Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”

MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

When I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he says, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”

Wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 issue of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

He points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he says. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.)

He loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.)

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” says Chalamet, a born and raised New Yorker.

We’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

“Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet says, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as important as the finished product.”

Next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.)

Chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a new daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet says. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”

SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”

And finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show currently on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet says. “I liked it in this little program I created.”

I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

Little provokes Chalamet more than the New York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he says, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

He tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to New York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he says, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”

DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”

Chalamet says he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”

On topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he says. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he says.

Leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

He’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get announced, I think you’ll see what I mean.”

Would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

Is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he says. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

Fashion Editor: Taylor McNeill. Hair and grooming products by Augustinus Bader. Grooming by Jamie Taylor. Produced on location by Object & Animal and Truenorth. For details, go to VF.com/credits.

Even the best reality TV shows can be accused of being scripted, and while not every claim is substantiated, there are a lot of allegations. Personally, like many others, I might be taken aback on the off chance that such a claim turns out to be true. Just recently, I found two stories from people who allegedly got a first-hand look at the inner workings of America's Got Talent and Bar Rescue, and they're fascinating to read.

AGT regularly draws claims online, with people alleging that it's scripted or faking parts of its programming. This latest claim from Reddit comes from someone who allegedly worked on the set and took issue with how one contestant's story was edited in the episode. Take a read:

I worked on America's Got Talent's 7th season and I never watched the show before working on it. I spent 4 days working, interviewing talented people with a camera crew and producer. I will not forget, we interviewed this one older woman who was a drummer. She was vibrant and friendly and we had a great talk, and then I watched when the episode aired and they recut the interview to make her seem flighty and mentally... off. Then she goes out on stage in front of the country for Sharon Osborne to mock her. It was bad, it was heartbreaking, that this woman's crime was 'older than 40 and good at drums' and the people making that show took liberty to destroy her on a national platform. They asked me to work on season 8 and I turned them down without a conversation.

It's not uncommon for reality TV show subjects to complain about receiving unflattering or dishonest edits. Over the years, stars have alleged that producers can get the response they want out of them and then edit the footage to make it appear they said something entirely different from what they meant. If AGT actually engaged in this, it wouldn't be different from claims against many other shows on the 2026 TV schedule. Regardless, this should be a gentle reminder for viewers not to believe everything they see.

The thread also revealed someone who was pretty upset with Bar Rescue after the show allegedly "ruined" one of his favorite locales. The renovation show is wildly popular and entertaining, but that doesn't always mean it's tackling bars that are in trouble. On that note, per the aforementioned user, his go-to bar didn't even need to be rescued:

This bar was packed ALL THE TIME. You drive by at 3 PM on a Tuesday, packed. 2 PM on a Sunday, packed. On more than one occasion, we had gone to the bar on a Friday or Saturday to find no place to sit because it was so full. They even bought the space next to them and knocked out a wall to make more room...Then we heard that Bar Rescue was coming. We wondered why they would need to 'rescue' this bar that was always full of people. But we got excited to see our bar on TV.

From there, the writer claimed the bar's owners removed all the furniture and revamped the menu with new cocktails. His wife apparently stood in line to attend the reopening and was instructed before entering that she could only order the signature cocktail.

When the Bar Rescue episode aired, it pushed the narrative that the cocktails were super popular and that "no one wants beer." As mentioned, attendees were allegedly told they could only purchase cocktails, which made it seem like the show's producers decided that would be the story before filming ever began. In the end, the "rescue" ended up ruining the bar, at least in this person's opinion:

People stopped going. Last time I went, it was a Friday night, and there were like 6 other people in the place. The bar ended up moving locations, and now I don't have a neighborhood place anymore. Fuck Bar Rescue.

The whole account really makes me rethink the times I've seen Jon Taffer give advice on how to fix a bar. Of course, this is all alleged, and it's not like there are receipts or concrete proof of these claims. It isn't necessarily hard to believe, but given the lack of hard evidence or even any identifiable information, I'd take it with a grain of salt.

While America's Got Talent and Bar Rescue aren't the only reality television shows accused of scripting their unscripted moments, they are two established legacy shows. I'm sure they won't be the last shows to be accused of being deceptive to the audience watching at home, but I'm not sure it'll actually keep anyone from watching.

The 2026 TV schedule is winding down, but there is still lots of good TV to watch. Even if it is reality television, there's no shortage of entertainment as we close out the year.

#3523. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3522. Magic: The Gathering’s New Commander Decks Offer Less for the Same Price

The four Commander decks for MTG Nauctis won't feature borderless Commander cards

The four Commander decks for MTG Nauctis won't feature borderless Commander cards

Magic: The Gathering players know it's an expensive hobby. Whether you're trying to keep up with a rapidly changing Standard format or you just want to add a spicy new card to your Commander deck, the hobby has surely gotten progressively more expensive. However, it's one thing to see product prices rise, and a completely different one to see that product lose some of its features while keeping the same price.

During MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, Wizards of the Coast officially presented Magic's latest set in a dedicated showcase, and I'm not talking about Star Trek, which saw its global launch that very weekend. Nauctis: The Sunken Realm is the next in-universe Magic set, scheduled for release on Feb. 5, 2027. Nauctis will introduce a brand-new, underwater world, and the set will feature a variety of products, as usual. This includes four Commander decks, but players have noticed that borderless Commander cards will no longer be included in the product, which is still being sold at a retail price of $49.99.

However, there is still a chance to get those fancy borderless Commander cards. The Premium Edition Commander Decks include one foil borderless face Commander and one foil borderless featured Commander. Plus, the entire deck is foil. However, the retail price for Premium Edition decks is $79.99. This means that players who really like having their borderless Commanders will have to shell out more money than usual, even if that comes with a full foil deck.

That's not the only controversial change that Nauctis will bring to Magic products. Starting with this set, Collector Boosters will drop from 15 cards to 12, while Standard Bundles will no longer feature foil full art lands, and the number of foil basic lands will drop from 15 to 10. Wizards of the Coast explained the reasoning behind some of the changes to make room for various printing experiments like God Packs, but many fans are understandably unhappy.

Nonetheless, the Nauctis Commander Decks at least seem exciting. The Boros (red-white) Seal the Deal has perhaps the best deck name in Magic history. The Bant (white-blue-green) Merfolk Regiment will add more options to one of the most popular typal decks in Magic. Izzet (blue-red) Blood in the Water has sharks. Need I say more? Finally, Sultai (green-blue-black) Terrors of the Abyss looks like the strongest option, if only because its two Commanders, the Ignoble Serpent and Zekes, Acid Rock Fan, have already been inadvertently spoiled on Scryfall.

Terrors of the Abyss's box features the phrases "discard and mill" and "reanimate sea monsters," and that seems to be a strong strategy, based on the deck's Commanders. The Ignoble Serpent costs eight mana (five colorless, one green, one blue, one black) for a 7/9 legendary serpent noble. Its text box reads:

At the beginning of your first upkeep in this game, if The Ignoble Serpent is in your command zone, mill four cards.

At the beginning of your end step, return target sea monster creature card from your graveyard to the battlefield. (Krakens, Leviathans, Octopuses, Serpents, and Whales are sea monsters.)

Commander players know how powerful passive abilities that activate while a Commander is in the Command Zone are, thanks to the infamous Eminence ability. This serpent starts its engine right away on turn one. If you can mill a powerful sea monster in the first four cards of your deck, then as soon as you play The Ignoble Serpent later in the game, that sea monster can hit the battlefield for free. And if you spend most of the game filling up your graveyard with other powerful sea monsters, then Ignoble Serpent's bottom ability makes it fairly easy to overwhelm opponents.

Some of my favorite picks for sea creatures to include in a deck like this would be the classic Simic Sky Swallower (featuring protection and evasion), The Terror of Serpent's Pass, the Unagi of Kiyoshi Island (which provides card draw). I'd be remiss not mentioning the terrific duo of Koma, Cosmos Serpent and Koma, World-Eater, two massive threats that are resilient to removal and also generate a scary number of creature tokens.

However, my favorite option is Sin, Spira's Punishment. When Sin enters or attacks, it makes a copy of another permanent in your graveyard. This means you could get two big monsters on the battlefield for the price of one. Sin can also make copies of lands, and it even draws a card in the process.

With 40 sea monsters in your deck, you have an 89% chance of milling one as part of those first four cards, but since it'll take you awhile to actually get The Ignoble Serpent onto the board, you have time to mill and/or discard sea monsters with cheap effects like Dark Matter Manipulator, Dream Twist, or Mental Note to ensure a big monster hits the battlefield every turn.

Overall, The Ignoble Serpent looks like a hugely powerful Commander, but not necessarily one that's overly game-breaking. Its viability will rely on a careful balance of ramp, mill, discard, and a big pile of nasty sea creatures.

#3521. Batman Forever's Director Nearly Rejected Jim Carrey As The Riddler Until He Saw This Movie

Say what you will about the "Batman" movies of the 1990s, there's no denying that they brought some truly massive star power to the screen. Even "Batman and Robin," often derided as the worst film of the entire franchise, was loaded with A-list actors, including Arnold Schwarzenegger, Uma Thurman, Alicia Silverstone, and a cameo appearance by the rapper Coolio. It was 1995's "Batman Forever," though, that gave the series what was arguably its biggest casting coup, when director Joel Schumacher cast Jim Carrey as the Riddler.

At the time, Carrey was experiencing a meteoric rise thanks to the success of "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and "Dumb and Dumber," which both released in 1994 and propelled him to the role of one of Hollywood's most prominent comedic actors. Looking back, putting him opposite Schumacher's campier Caped Crusader seems like a natural fit. Initially, however, Schumacher thought Carrey was simply too young to play the part. As revealed in a 1994 interview with "Comics Scene," the director only changed his mind when he saw Carrey bring another comic book to life on the big scree. As Carrey told the magazine, Schumacher "thought I was a little too young. Then, when he saw the trailer for 'The Mask,' he changed his mind."

While it went through some significant changes on its way to becoming a film — mostly to tone down the violence that made director Chuck Russell initially think of it as a horror movie and add in way more swing dancing — "The Mask" started out as a comic book by writer John Arcudi and artist Doug Mahnke. Carrey, whose over-the-top delivery and exaggerated impressions made him a breakout star on the sketch comedy show "In Living Color," was the perfect fit for the cartoonish, chaotic madman that emerged when the power of the trickster god Loki wound up in the hands of a relatively lovable loser.

Although he allegedly had a much longer cut of the film that skewed darker and more serious than the final result, Schumacher's take on Batman was heavily influenced by the 1960s TV show, so it makes sense that he'd look for a comic actor to play the Riddler. Long before the Riddler was the dark and murderous villain of "The Batman," he was one of the Dark Knight's sillier foes. Frank Gorshin, who played the Riddler to perfection on that show, was a well-known comedian and impressionist himself, and before Carrey's casting, Robin Williams was considered to be a favorite for the part. Seeing Carrey pull off the menacing silliness of "The Mask" and make that film a huge hit likely did a lot to sell Schumacher on giving Carrey a chance — and the fact that Carrey did it while wearing a lot of green probably didn't hurt either.

As for how it worked out, well, Carrey's performance as Edward Nygma in "Batman Forever" was, to put it charitably, a lot. The Riddler was undoubtedly annoying on purpose, but Carrey into being straight-up grating. Even his co-star thought so, with Tommy Lee Jones (who played Two-Face in the film) famously telling him "I cannot sanction your buffoonery" when they met.

That said, there are some really great parts of his performance, too. While the Riddler was way over the top, the way Carrey plays Edward Nygma as an obsessive fanboy of Val Kilmer's Bruce Wayne, including a scene where he dresses like Wayne down to the glasses while showing off his mind-controlling invention, is actually really solid. It's also the kind of subtle — well, subtle for Carrey, at least — touch that only really worked because of Carrey's youth.

#3519. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3518. James Bond: How Old Every 007 Actor Was In Their First And Last Movies

Following a lengthy casting process that, at times, felt like it might never come to an end, Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond. The director of the upcoming 26th Bond installment, Denis Villeneuve, and the new custodian of the 007 franchise, Amazon MGM, have opted for one of the most consistently interesting actors working today, and it will be fascinating to see what the "Primetime" star does as England's greatest spy.

Pattinson's casting as Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of relative unknowns taking on the role. The British actor is one of the biggest stars in the world — which, again, means Amazon MGM shouldn't have to worry too much about box office profits. But he's also one of the most exciting actors of his generation and has been delivering fascinating performances ever since he joined the Safdie Brothers for 2017's "Good Time."

As such, Pattinson's age is surely of little consequence. We know the man can deliver, and everyone should be looking forward to seeing what choices he makes in a role he's described as a "dream come true." But with Amazon MGM likely eyeing a 2028 release date for Pattinson's 007 debut, we've got plenty of time to kill. So, why not take a look at how he measures up to the other Bond actors in terms of age? Here are all the James Bond actors' ages in their first and last 007 movies.

In 1962, "Dr. No kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise," introducing audiences to a rugged young Scotsman by the name of Sean Connery. The actor was born on August 25, 1930, which means he was 31 when filming on "Dr. No" got underway in January 1962. By the time the movie hit theaters in October of that year, he was 32.

Director Terrence Young's urbane manner helped mold Connery's rough-around-the edges Bond into the legendary cinematic figure we remember today. By the time he made his last appearance in the tux for 1971's "Diamonds are Forever," however, he needed no help whatsoever. Filming began in April 1971 when Connery was 40. The film debuted in December of that year, by which point the actor — who passed away in 2020 — was 41, the same age Robert Pattinson will likely be by the time his Bond movie starts shooting. A 52-year-old Connery returned for an unofficial Bond entry in 1983's "Never Say Never Again."

George Lazenby is the only James Bond actor to only appear in the role once. Thankfully, his sole outing as 007 was one of the best Bond movies ever made. 1969's "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" was a brilliant installment in the franchise and is Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond film. Considering Lazenby was following in Sean Connery's footsteps, that's a pretty impressive accomplishment.

Born on September 5, 1939, the Australian model-turned-actor was 29 when filming on "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" began in October 1968. By the time the film debuted in December 1969, Lazenby had turned 30. That was it for the Aussie star, who's still going strong today at the age of 87. "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" was his first and only Bond outing, and Lazenby remains the youngest ever actor to play the role.

After Sean Connery's brief return as James Bond in "Diamonds Are Forever" Roger Moore donned the tux for 1973's "Live and Let Die." The British actor was born on October 14, 1927. Almost exactly 45 years later, his first Bond outing began shooting on October 13, 1972, making him 44 when production started and 45 by the time the movie debuted in June 1973.

That made him older than both Connery and George Lazenby, regardless of whether we're talking their first or last 007 movie. Today, he's still the oldest actor ever cast as James Bond.

Moore retired from the Bond saga with his seventh appearance in the role. He was 57 when "A View to a Kill" bowed in May 1985, and all too aware of his age. The actor told Entertainment Weekly: "I became very conscious that I was getting long in the tooth to play the great lover." More than 40 years later, Moore remains the oldest actor to ever portray Bond.

Next to George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton is surely the most underrated of all the James Bond actors. He brought a darkness to the character long before Daniel Craig's tortured spy debuted, and his interpretation of Bond remains one of the most interesting in the series' history.

The actor was born in Wales on March 21, 1946, making him 40 years old when filming got underway on 1987's "The Living Daylights." When the film opened in July 1987 in the United States, Dalton was 41. He only portrayed Bond in one other film, 1989's "Licence to Kill," and was 42 when filming commenced in July 1988. The movie hit theaters in July 1989, by which time he was 43. Dalton almost played Bond again in 1995's "GoldenEye," but the film took some time to come together and when it did, former Bond custodians EON Productions had found someone new.

After Timothy Dalton's brief James Bond tenure came to an end, EON tapped a dashing young Irishman by the name of Pierce Brosnan to be his successor. 1995's "GoldenEye" is a pretty silly movie viewed in retrospect, but it will remain forever legendary for capturing the imagination of a whole new generation of Bond fans, who quickly became further enraptured by the video game tie-in.

Brosnan was born May 16, 1953, making him 41 when "GoldenEye" filming began in January 1995. The film bowed in theaters in November of that year, by which time he had turned 42 — just a year younger than Dalton in his final Bond performance.

Seven years later, Brosnan made his fourth and final appearance as 007 in "Die Another Day," which makes "GoldenEye" look like a work of pure artistic genius in comparison. Brosnan's now infamous final turn as 007 (it's the worst Bond film according to IMDb) started shooting in January 2002, at which point the actor was 48. When it hit theaters in November of that year he'd turned 49 and was well and truly done with the Bond franchise.

Daniel Craig will always be in contention for the title of best James Bond simply because he starred in the best James Bond movie ever made: 2006's "Casino Royale." Craig was born on March 2, 1968, and was 37 when filming began in January of 2006. That makes him the third youngest Bond to be cast in the role. He was 38 when "Casino Royale" arrived in theaters in November 2006.

Sadly, Craig's Bond tenure was characterized by diminishing returns and things went badly awry with 2021's "No Time to Die." Craig had clearly had enough by that point, too. The actor was 51 when filming started in April 2019, and 53 when the film was released in October 2021. It marked his fifth and final time playing Bond, and saw him become the second-oldest actor to ever portray the character after Roger Moore.

So, we come to the man himself. Robert Pattinson is now officially set to debut as James Bond in Denis Villeneuve's upcoming film. Just what the director has planned remains a mystery at this point, but casting Pattinson is a great start.

The actor beat out other finalists including Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult, to take the coveted role as England's greatest spy. Interestingly enough, he was the oldest of the bunch. The British actor was born on May 13 1986, making him 40 years old at the time he was cast as 007. The movie will likely start shooting in early 2027, so he will either be 40 or 41 at the time of filming. That puts Pattinson in the middle of the pack in terms of every Bond actor's age at the time of their casting.

Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with a mix of excitement and trepidation at what many see as a fairly safe choice. Those who've been following his career, however, should have no doubt he'll deliver in his Bond debut.
