I absolutely loved Channing Tatum's Gambit in Deadpool & Wolverine. His ridiculous Cajun accent, the way Ryan Reynolds' Deadpool couldn't understand half of what he was saying, and the fact that Tatum finally got to play the character after years of trying made his appearance one of my favorite parts of the movie. But with Gambit returning for Avengers: Doomsday on the 2026 movie schedule, I've been wondering whether Marvel would give him more to do than make everybody laugh. Thankfully, Kevin Feige has some reassuring news.

Speaking with Empire about the upcoming Marvel movie and the return of the original Fox-era X-Men, the Marvel Studios president discussed what audiences can expect from Tatum's Remy LeBeau. And it sounds like the character will have considerably more going on this time around. According to Feige:

He's a standout. It's fun to see Gambit be as charismatic as he was in Deadpool & Wolverine, and yet in Doomsday it's not all for laughs. He's a fully-rounded character.

That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. Don't get me wrong, I laughed every time Gambit opened his mouth in Deadpool & Wolverine. Watching the Merc with the Mouth struggle to decipher his thick accent was hilarious, especially when he asked whether the Minions were his dialect coach. But I also want to see Tatum get a chance to actually play Gambit as a full-fledged character. After all, the mutant hero has quite a bit more going for him than an accent and a deck of exploding playing cards.

In the comics, Remy LeBeau is a former thief with a complicated past, and his relationship with Rogue remains one of the X-Men's most recognizable romances. There's plenty for Marvel to work with. Considering how long Tatum fought to play him, I'd hate to see the character reduced to merely comic relief.

For years, the actor tried to get a standalone Gambit movie made at 20th Century Fox. The project went through numerous delays and creative changes before Disney acquired the studio, and the film was ultimately canceled. Then Ryan Reynolds helped bring Tatum's version of the mutant to life in 2024, finally giving him the opportunity he'd been chasing for the better part of a decade.

Tatum has already said his approach to Gambit would change for Doomsday. He previously explained that directors Anthony and Joe Russo wanted him to dial back the exaggerated Cajun accent, allowing the character to have more serious moments without losing what made his introduction so entertaining.

With that in mind, Feige's latest comments become particularly encouraging. It's one thing to promise a slightly more understandable Gambit, but hearing that Marvel considers him a standout character suggests they're giving the 21 Jump Street star room to explore another side of Remy.

The Gambit-Related Mistake Channing Tatum Nearly Made: ‘It Would’ve Just Been A Catastrophe’

Of course, there's still plenty we don't know about his role in the epic comic book movie. Doomsday is bringing back several familiar X-Men, including James Marsden's Cyclops, Ian McKellen's Magneto and Patrick Stewart's Professor X. Empire also revealed a new look at Gambit alongside Cyclops outside the X-Mansion, which is pretty cool considering Tatum never got to appear alongside the original team during Fox's run. With Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom threatening the multiverse, I imagine there will be plenty of opportunities for Gambit to put those playing cards to work.

I'm excited to see what Tatum does with a character he clearly loves, especially now that he gets another opportunity to play him. Keep the charm, let him crack a few jokes, and maybe give the guy a few standout character moments that audiences won't soon forget. That's not asking too much, is it?

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters Dec. 18. But until then, fans can revisit Gambit's appearance in Deadpool & Wolverine, streaming with a Disney+ subscription.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3515. Christopher Nolan Helped Rescue Theaters — Now He Could Save Physical Media

Whether or not you're a fan of the films of Christopher Nolan, there's a lot to appreciate about him, especially for cinephiles. Chief among his virtues is his dedication to celluloid itself, as he's been instrumental in helping physical film stay alive, both for shooting and exhibiting features. The rise of Premium Large Format screens can be directly linked to his embrace of IMAX, too. Both of these facts have heavily contributed to the rescue of movie theatergoing, which seemed inevitably doomed in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Thanks to Nolan setting an example and others in the industry following his lead, we have a newly robust theatrical exhibition landscape which only continues to improve.

This influential power of Nolan's may now be extending to the cause of physical media. The filmmaker has long been a proponent of films being made available for purchase on disc. In fact, he said as much in November 2023, which coincidentally was just a month after the retail giant Best Buy publicly announced it would be discontinuing the sale of physical media movies in its online and physical stores. Cut to this week, where it appears this tide may be turning: Employees and fans have shared that Best Buy will be selling physical copies of Nolan's "The Odyssey" in its stores, marking the first time since 2023 that the company has reneged on its stance.

While this could be a mere one-off incident, it's more likely Best Buy is dipping its toes back into the water of selling movies again. If this move is successful, it would mean that Nolan has once again helped save films and film culture from the scourge of corporations and the tech industry trying to fix something that wasn't broken.

On paper, it makes all the sense in the world for Best Buy to make "The Odyssey" 4K UHDs available for purchase. The film is one of the biggest hits of 2026, and could be on its way to some nominations (if not wins) at the Academy Awards. Other competitors like Walmart still sell physical media in their locations, and have never stopped. It's also the Christmas shopping season, and movies on disc are a great holiday gift for many.

For now, it seems Best Buy will only be selling the 4K version of "The Odyssey" — the Premium Giftset edition and other formats like a Steelbook appear to be sold via online retailers only. Yet while the retailer may not be catering to hardcore physical media collectors as it used to during its heyday, Best Buy reinstating the sale of physical movies, even on a limited basis for now, is a big deal.

What's undeniable is how this choice on the part of the company is as good an indicator as any that the market for physical media is alive and well. Sure, most average folks have been trained to utilize streaming services as their primary source of entertainment, yet the recent issues that have cropped up with digital-only services (particularly in the gaming world) have made even casual disc buyers more interested in rebuilding their collections. While the physical media market has a long way to go to recapture its former glory (and may never reach those heights again), it's so wonderful to see folks like Nolan put their weight behind keeping discs alive. How fitting that "The Odyssey" is the release where physical media at Best Buy finally returns in a big way.

During a press conference, Swift discussed (via Hello!) the acclaimed movie’s theme of friendship and stressed the importance of someone looking back on such intimate bonds. She also said this:

You may feel, ‘Oh, that friend I had, that was really a special time, and even though I don't know that person anymore, I hope they're doing great,’ or feeling like you could count on your friends to be there when you needed them; feeling like you don't need to have a million of the wrong friends.

The “Delicate” performer’s comments fall directly in line with the narrative of the new Toy Story film, which sees young Bonnie attempting to make genuine friendships. At the same time, cowgirl doll Jessie also reflects fondly on the bond she had with her former owner, Emily. Those plot threads culminated into a truly sentimental third act for the billion-dollar-grossing film. Aside from that, though, Swift’s thoughts are indeed sweet, and they do speak to the nature of how friends come in and out of our lives as time goes on.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

To give that moment the respect it deserves, the episode is getting a theatrical release.

The show's official X account announced this on Nov. 16, sharing a link where fans can find local theaters with screenings. As an added bonus, the cinematic event will actually be an early release of season 3's episode 7, as the screenings will take place on Nov. 23 and 24.

This isn't the first time Amazon has brought one of its original Prime Video series to the big screen, as The Boys' finale also received the treatment earlier this year. As for the actual conclusion to season 3, fans will have to be satisfied seeing that on their TV, phones, or tablets.

Since the start of season 3, audiences have been waiting for Sauron to forge the One Ring. The season, which began with a five-year time jump that serves as a soft reboot of the show, has heavily focused on the villain's attempts to finally create his all-powerful weapon. His failure to do so up to this point has largely been due to the lack of help from the Elven smith Celebrimbor, who forged the rings of power for the dwarves, men, and elves.

The One Ring is arguably the most important object in all of Middle-earth, as it features in Tolkien's novel The Hobbit as well as being the main McGuffin of the original Lord of the Rings trilogy. While we've caught glimpses of its forging in Peter Jackson's films, Rings of Power will be the first time we've seen the entire process in all its glory. If you don't mind the changes the show made to the source material, then this will surely be a moment worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

#3510. Jet Li And Morgan Freeman's Forgotten Martial Arts Movie Is Worth Revisiting

Louis Leterrier's 2005 action flick "Unleashed," written by Luc Besson, is a fun, intense, somewhat strange vehicle for martial arts superstar Jet Li. In the film, Li plays Danny, a vicious bodyguard for a Glasgow gangster named Bart (Bob Hoskins). Bart has mentally conditioned Danny to remain calm and obedient when he is wearing a metal collar, but he turns feral and deadly when Bart takes the collar off. Danny is a "dog" and, occasionally, he is literally unleashed.

Meanwhile, Morgan Freeman co-stars as Sam, a blind pianist who takes Danny into his home after he gets separated from Bart during a "dogfighting" tournament. Sam and his stepdaughter Victoria (Kerry Condon) then raise Danny to be more gentle and humane and, in time, are able to remove his collar without Danny becoming violent. Because of this, Danny begins to remember his past and develops an interest in music, finding his humanity again. Naturally, though, Bart eventually re-emerges in Danny's life, leaving him torn between his newfound family and the violence he was conditioned to live in.

"Unleashed" has everything you might want from a Saturday afternoon matinee. It has recognizable movie stars, it sports a pretty good performance by Li, and it features works by the always reliable Freeman and Hoskins, as well as the somewhat under-appreciated Condon. There's a reason /Film previously listed it as an underrated martial arts movie, as well as one of Li's top 10 best movies in general.

The film also doesn't forget that it has to be at least 40% martial arts scenes to justify casting Li, with legendary martial arts choreographer Yuen Woo-Ping providing its fight choreography. It was hardly a hit, but "Unleashed" is certainly worth tracking down.

It's worth pausing to note that "Unleashed," aesthetically speaking, is very much a product of its time. Pierre Morel's cinematography has the green-tint and artificially enhanced grain that was so in vogue in the 2000s (along with several harshly-lit scenes), while the film is edited by Nicolas Trembasiewicz in a haphazard and swift style that will make your head spin. To be sure, "Unleashed" very much bears a distinctly mid-'00s action aesthetic.

Additionally, the film's score was provided by trip hop collective Massive Attack and produced by the RZA. Its soundtrack was originally released under the title "Danny the Dog," and it mostly consists of electronic and/or ambient beats. This only further dates "Unleashed," adding to what one might call its "2000s edgelord" design.

But in spite of this, "Unleashed" remains grounded thanks to Jet Li's amazing performance and Morgan Freeman's gentle confidence. Kerry Condon also brings a childlike innocence to the movie as Victoria, giving Danny someone to relate to. Condon was in her early 20s when "Unleashed" was made, but the film gives her braces and a youthful demeanor, creating the impression that her character might be a high schooler.

Above it all, "Unleashed" is an effective melodrama. When Danny begins to remember his past late in the film, he recalls the deep tragedy of his upbringing and the dark circumstances that led him into the thrall of the evil Bart to begin with. Indeed, Bob Hoskins is so good at playing heavies and gangsters that he infuses "Unleashed" with a good amount of menace. (Bart is not a good guy by any stretch of the imagination.)

Critics generally liked "Unleashed," with the larger critical consensus being that "Unleashed" is "good enough." Many of the film's reviews similarly cite its performances and humanity as key elements that offsets its fighting and violence.

Case in point: Roger Ebert gave the movie three stars out of four, writing that its story was familiar and that it "could have made a laughable movie. That it works is because of the performances of Jet Li and Bob Hoskins, who plays his master." He added:

"The film is ingenious in its construction. It has all the martial arts action any Jet Li fan could possibly desire, choreographed by Yeun Woo-ping, who is the Gerald Arpino of kung-fu and creates improbable but delightful ballets of chops and socks, leaps and twists and kicks and improvisations. Everything happens in a denatured sepia tone that is not black and white nor quite color, but a palette drained of cheer and pressing down like a foggy day."

(Gerald Arpino, for those unfamiliar with the name, was a famed ballet dancer and choreographer who was head of the Joffrey Ballet for decades.)

Ebert is spot-on with his observation about the denatured sepia of "Unleashed." Everything does feel depressive as a result. When it comes to actioners like this, though, "better than average" can actually serve as high praise. Unlike many other action films, you might actually remember this one.

#3508. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3507. 26 Years Later, The Grinch's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Christmas Movie Quote Ever

Since its publication back in 1957, author Theodor "Dr. Seuss" Geisel's illustrated children's book "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!" has become a universally treasured tale about the deeper spiritual meaning of the titular winter holiday. Then, when directors Chuck Jones and Ben Washam adapted Seuss' gently whimsical work into an animated TV special in 1966, the result was an equally enchanting bit of merriment featuring quite the festive earworm in the form of "You're a Mean One, Mr. Grinch."

The Ron Howard-helmed 2000 blockbuster "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," on the other hand, is anything but gentle in its quirkiness. While Michael Corenblith's production design for the live-action film brings the settings of Seuss' source material to fittingly wayward and fanciful life on-screen, Howard and his cinematographer Donald Peterman shoot the action in a visually hectic fashion, filtering the bright colors of its costumes and sets in a way that makes everything look kinda hazy. All the while, Jim Carrey doesn't so much nibble as devour the scenery with his portrayal of the Grinch, who behaves less like the curmudgeon that Seuss first imagined and more like an insecure chaos goblin.

As we now know, Carrey used actual CIA-approved torture-resistance techniques to tolerate the (admittedly, astonishing) prosthetics he wore for the role, which explains why his performance is so cartoonish and otherwise in-your-face, even by the "Ace Ventura" and "Dumb and Dumber" actor's standards (not to mention, how he drove makeup artist Kazuhiro Tsuji to seek therapy after completing his work on the film). Add in the movie's sometimes incredibly adult humor (including an infamous romantic subplot involving the Grinch himself), and it's not hard to see why Howard's adaptation tends to be polarizing. Still, to its credit, it does justice to perhaps the most important quote from Seuss' classic.

In the climax of Ron Howard's "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" (just like in Dr. Seuss' original book), the Grinch has, true to his word, stolen the assorted Christmas decorations, presents, and other trinkets from his neighbors down in Whoville. But just as he's about to chuck them all off the top of a mountain (one Mount Crumpit, to be exact), he looks down and spots the Whos happily singing and enjoying themselves all the same. It's then that the film's unnamed narrator (Anthony Hopkins) and the Grinch observe: "Maybe Christmas, he thought, doesn't come from a store. Maybe Christmas, perhaps, means a little bit more."

At its core, this line is a simple yet elegant way of reminding everyone that Christmas is about showing love and affection towards the world around them. Yet, it's also a clear rejection of the rampant consumerism and materialism that has come to be associated with the holiday, which itself speaks to the capitalist critique that's always existed at the heart of Seuss' rhythmic fable.

If anything, Howard's movie doubles down on this message by adding a subplot in which Cindy Lou Who (Taylor Momsen) — the precocious Who responsible for setting the Grinch's eventual transformation in motion — finds herself feeling disillusioned about Christmas. The other Whos, you see, have become so fixated on the commercial side of the holiday that they've lost sight of what they're even meant to be celebrating, and it's only thanks to the Grinch that they come to see the error of their ways. Like so much of Howard's film, we can debate whether this is a truly necessary addition to Seuss' story, but it certainly doesn't undermine what he was going for to begin with.

It’s been very clear from the opening (express pass-oriented) episode of The Amazing Race 39 that producers were hoping for an all-women team to win. The season started out with five all-women teams, and subsequent episodes have noted various milestones the ladies have hit and more. On one level, it’s been nice to see so many ladies in the mix. Yet, because of the way gameplay has been set up, the same mixed gender teams were targeted myriad times, and that has meant two INCREDIBLE teams have not really being treated as threats.

I'm about to get into spoiler's for last week's "Million Dollar Moves" episode on the 2026 TV schedule, including who was eliminated, so heads up! Still with me? Great.

Hear me out, because I’m about to semi-talk some smack about the games Ali & Joanna and Anne-Marie & Riley have played, and I want to make it clear I like both teams. They’re good TV. They’re strong competitors. I especially appreciate the likable personalities both teams have exhibited. The soccer pals and mother-daughter duo have great respect for their partners, but because of the way the new season was put together and edited they have just skated by.

Because Ali & Joanna aligned with Ann-Marie & Riley early on, they’ve had a big advantage compared to a lot of other teams. I don’t think anyone is really on the look out for them, either, despite the fact both teams have earned a first place finish twice. They are threats, but because the mixed gender team of Michelle & Matt was highlighted as “the big threat” and went on a midseason three-episode winning tear, these other two teams have stayed under the radar.

Listen, I feel like The Amazing Race producers knew Matt & Michelle would be targeted in the double U-Turn, but they and Daisha and Dalton prevailed anyway during that first live round. Then, the next week they set up a second double U-Turn, and of course Matt & Michelle were targeted again. Phil called the couple “dynamic” in this BTS Race video, and given how fun they were to watch, I wish things would have shaken out a bit differently so another (or other) teams were targeted that second episode, but that is what it is.

The bigger problem, however? The way the challenge was set up led to all of the other teams working together. Everyone huddled together and gave each other answers like they were cheating on a pop quiz, and then Matt & Michelle had to go it alone. They also had to do both sides of the challenge with no help. Yes, struggling with directions didn’t help, but they were at a heavy disadvantage due to being targeted. The other teams weren’t.

I’m sure TAR would call it fair gameplay. I call it boring TV.

The thing is, as a former soccer player myself, I get the competitive attitude, and I’d love to see Ali & Joanna win. I’ve actually felt that way even before Michelle & Matt started dominating. I think it’s probably a strength for the two leading lady teams they’re both just skating by under-the-radar this season. If I were them, I’d be extremely happy about this outcome and the way the show has ultimately set them up for success.

I honestly more blame the set up of the race this season for creating a non-compelling narrative. Allowing teams to “work together” has been a point of contention on The Amazing Race for a long time. (Like I can remember a major incident back in Season 32, so years, and producers have even discussed making changes before.)

There’s always a question of “where is the line,” right? Is it OK to give another team directions or point them in the right direction with a clue? I’d argue yes. Is it OK to work together on a detail-oriented counting challenge 100% so that the colluding teams all finish together? Even if the Race says that’s fine, I’d argue those episodes make the show go from a 9/10 to a 2/10 for those who are watching.

Just something to consider, Race producers.

Anyway, this “working together” philosophy has certainly helped Ali & Joanna and Ann-Marie & Riley get through a lot of challenges this season, and they’ve managed to do it with most of the other teams being none the wiser, or at least not seeing them as real threats to win. There's a lot of money at stake, and per TAR’s rules, they aren’t doing anything wrong. Still, if an all-women team wins this season, I would have liked it way better if they’d done it on their own merit, and not because of some Amazing Race challenge loopholes.

#3504. Jennifer Connelly's Forgotten '90s Disney Superhero Movie Deserved Its Own Franchise

After Tim Burton's "Batman" film became an inescapably huge success in the summer of 1989 and set off to expand into its weirdly experimental sequel in 1992, there was a mad rush by other studios to hop a trend and get their own piece of that lucrative superhero pie — sort of. Studio executives of the early '90s seem to have been drawn more to Burton's retro aesthetics than the actual idea of a superhero, so rather than expanding into bringing other iconic DC characters like Wonder Woman to the big screen, or heading across the street to give the Marvel universe a shot at cinematic glory, we got a rush of big-screen revivals of other throwback comic strip heroes. The results were, well, let's just put it nicely and say they were pretty mixed in terms of quality.

While they undoubtedly have their fans out there, pulp hero movies like 1990's "Dick Tracy," 1994's "The Shadow," and 1996's "The Phantom" simply were not able to reach the same levels of success. It may have been that audiences just liked Batman way more than they liked characters who had never been as popular as the Caped Crusader, or that these movies just weren't very good. Maybe people were just simply not prepared to slam evil. Whatever it was, none of those movies managed to launch their heroes into a franchise.

There is, however, one member of that crowd that absolutely deserved better: 1991's "The Rocketeer," in which Jennifer Connelly, Billy Campbell, and a rocket-powered jetpack faced off against Nazis in Los Angeles circa 1938.

One big difference that set "The Rocketeer" apart from the surrounding crop of pulp hero flicks was that its source material was actually pretty contemporary. Cliff Secord and his supporting cast were created in 1982 by the legendary comics creator Dave Stevens, and had been an indie favorite since its introduction. All things considered, Stevens produced a relatively small number of comics about the Rocketeer — his entire run with the character fits into a single 120-page hardcover — but his lavish, gorgeous art and incredible storytelling make it a timeless classic even today. Sadly, Stevens passed away in 2008 after a long battle with leukemia, which had long affected his output.

Looking back, it's easy to see why Disney jumped on "The Rocketeer." Since it was a throwback to the adventure serials and comic strip heroes of the '30s and '40s, Stevens' work already had the modern spin on the kind of pulpy action that movies like "Dick Tracy" and "The Shadow" struggled with, and incorporated a lot of the same elements. In fact, the "Rocketeer" comics even included thinly veiled versions of pulp heroes like The Shadow and Doc Savage in supporting roles, with just enough of their serial numbers filed off to avoid a copyright lawsuit. (Needless to say, those characters didn't make it into the film version.)

There were real-life influences, too; in the film, the jetpack was created by Howard Hughes, and Timothy Dalton's villainous Neville Sinclair was based on actor (and real-life villain) Errol Flynn. Connelly's character, appropriately renamed Jenny, was based on Cliff's comics girlfriend Betty, who was in turn inspired by pin-up icon Bettie Page, of whom Stevens was a dedicated and unabashed fan.

As for the film, while it lacks the lushness of Stevens' comics art, it told the classic story of "boy loves girl, boy finds rocket pack, boy has to rescue girl from an evil Nazi actor played by one of the lesser James Bonds" in a fun, engaging way that made it a cult classic. It also has a connection to the modern Marvel Cinematic Universe. Two decades after "The Rocketeer," its director, Joe Johnston, would direct another, more successful retro-inspired superhero movie, 2011's "Captain America: The First Avenger."

According to an interview with Stevens, the original plan for "The Rocketeer" had been to make a trilogy that would've skewed slightly more adult:

"So, we had a lot of interesting meetings with executives who passed on it but gave us some good criticisms. The last studio on the list was Disney. They took one look at it, and said 'toys!' So ... that's where we eventually made the deal. We originally signed on as a trilogy at Touchstone, the division of Disney doing more adult-themed films. [...] As soon as we all signed on, [Disney executive Jeffrey] Katzenberg pulled a switch and said, 'Nope, it's going to be a Disney release, because Disney needs a live-action hit.' So immediately, Betty and anything else "adult" went right out with the bathwater."

We'll never know if a more adult-oriented version of "The Rocketeer" that kept elements like Betty's glamour modeling day job intact would've been successful enough to get us that trilogy, but the movie we got is well worth revisiting, even though it was crushed by "Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves" and "Terminator 2" at the box office.

When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3501. Netflix Adds The 2026 Horror Movie That Made Over 500x Its Budget At The Box Office

"Obsession" passed a box office milestone only five other horror films ever have when it crossed the $500 million mark. That would be an achievement regardless of its budget, but this movie only cost $600,000 to $750,000 to make. That means that when "Obsession" brought in $524.4 million by the end of its unprecedented box office run, it had made more than 500 times its budget.

For a while, that made "Obsession" the most profitable movie ever at the box office, until it was technically dethroned by the low-budget Chinese movie "Niu Lai." Still, it remains one of the most stunning horror success stories of recent years, which is especially impressive considering we've seen multiple low-budget horror movies become hits of late. But if you somehow managed to miss out on all of this, or just want to revisit one of the best horror movies of 2026, Netflix has you covered.

"Obsession" has a relatively simple premise, yet its execution and the lead performances elevate it beyond your typical low-budget horror fare. The film stars Michael Johnston as Baron "Bear" Bailey, a luckless music store worker who has a major crush on his friend/co-worker Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After buying a One Wish Willow toy, he wishes that Nikki loved him more than anyone in the world and gets everything he asked for and more. The only problem is, Nikki becomes absolutely obsessed with him, to the extent she's willing to hurt anyone who gets in her way.

It's well worth doing so. "Obsession" is a confident crowd-pleaser with a killer lead performance from Navarette. In fact the actor's portrayal of Nikki proved to be her breakout turn, landing Navarrette a role as Rogue in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's upcoming "X-Men" movie reboot. No doubt, more high-profile roles await. As such, even if you're not too intrigued by the prospect of a twisted girlfriend causing violent chaos, you should at least check out "Obsession" to see one of the best performances of 2026 and the beginning of a star's ascendence. The film is streaming on Netflix as of November 17, 2026.

#3500. Magic: The Gathering Designer Says Commander’s Most Divisive Staple Isn’t Going Anywhere

Commander’s “foundational, iconic heart” is here to stay

The two best T-shirts I saw at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026 were easy to choose in a sea of delightfully nerdy references and imagery. One was black with a wall of white text spelling out the lengthy definition of Banding, a notoriously confusing Magic: The Gathering mechanic that’s now 33 years old. The other was a white shirt featuring a picture of a Sol Ring card crossed out by a red circle and slash. “BAN SOL RING,” it read.

The first shirt provides a public service and a punchline about ancient Magic history. Based on an interview conducted at MagicCon, the second is a bold demand that Magic principal designer Gavin Verhey has no interest in entertaining.

“Sol Ring is the foundational, iconic heart of the format,” Verhey tells Polygon.

Commander’s most ubiquitous artifact, Sol Ring, costs one colorless mana and taps to produce two colorless mana. There are few Commander experiences more satisfying than drawing one to start the game, allowing you to drop it on the first turn (and maybe even follow that up with an Arcane Signet). Suddenly, your deck’s strategy accelerates. If you have a four-cost Commander, they’re out on turn two. But no matter the cost of your Commander or what your deck wants to do, Sol Ring is going to help it all happen sooner.

I never want to see another turn-one Sol Ring again

That ruthless efficiency is also a reason to ban it. An early Sol Ring can give one player a major advantage, forcing everyone else to either catch up or collectively deal with the person who drew it. Its near-universal usefulness also eats up a slot that could otherwise go toward something more directly tied to a distinctive strategy. Verhey recognizes the card’s power. He just sees its place in Commander differently.

“It’s been in basically every single Commander precon we’ve ever made,” he says. “It’s in almost every Commander deck players build. People love it, and they love their unique variations of Sol Ring.”

There are 146 individual printings of the card, with 75 unique pieces of artwork. One features Garfield the cat dancing with his beloved Arlene. Another depicts Dogmeat from the Fallout franchise staring at his reflection in a bowl of water. Many, including the oldest, show a bright ring of light in the midst of a blazing inferno.

In a casual, four-player format, Verhey argues, the possibility of someone getting an explosive start thanks to a Sol Ring can help make individual games feel different. In a 100-card singleton format like Commander, you have a 7.46% chance of drawing one, so that is actually quite rare. Everyone has access to the same card, but who draws it — and what the rest of the table does about it — changes from game to game.

“I think it actually creates dynamic Commander games a lot of the time,” Verhey says. “You played Sol Ring on turn one. We all see that threat, right? We all know who the enemy is.”

For Sol Ring’s critics, the early advantage and ensuing dogpile are part of the problem. For Verhey, they can be part of the fun: an immediate complication that gives three other players something to respond to.

“Is it incredibly strong? Absolutely,” he says. “Is it necessarily the poster child I would have chosen if I was creating Commander from scratch? Probably not.”

But Commander already exists, and Sol Ring is deeply embedded in it. Verhey doesn’t foresee challenging that status “at any point.”

Still, it has at least been considered in the past. When the former Commander Rules Committee banned Mana Crypt, Jeweled Lotus, and Dockside Extortionist in September 2024, it explicitly acknowledged that Sol Ring met its criteria for a ban. The committee nevertheless made an exception because removing the card would fundamentally change the format’s identity.

There’s room to disagree about whether that distinction makes a turn-one Sol Ring an enjoyable gameplay experience. But preserving variety in Commander doesn’t mean eliminating every staple just because everybody uses it. For now, and probably forever, if you’re the type of person who’s going to show up at MagicCon with a “Ban Sol Ring” shirt, then you’re just going to have to ban it within your pod.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3498. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3497. 5 Reasons Why Robert Pattinson Could Be The Best James Bond Yet

Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, beating out several promising contenders to take the coveted role. Denis Villeneuve will oversee the upcoming 26th Bond installment, and he couldn't have chosen a more dynamic and interesting leading man.

Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with both excitement and wariness — which is to be expected. After all, the British actor is one of the biggest stars in Hollywood and is therefore unlike any actor to be cast in the role throughout the franchise's more than 60-year history. But clearly Villeneuve and new Bond custodians Amazon MGM have been impressed by the actor, and frankly it's not hard to see why.

The "Primetime" star has been delivering consistently compelling performances for years now, and if nothing else it will be fascinating to see what he does to make England's greatest spy his own. Sure, on the surface he seems like a safe choice — A-lister white guy with a string of hits to his name. But part of what makes Pattinson so exciting as an actor is his unpredictability. Beyond that, there are myriad reasons why he could not only make a great 007, but might just give us the best Bond yet. Here are five of them.

Robert Pattinson is a big star with the kind of look you'd associate with James Bond. But he's made no secret of the fact he's also a bit of a weirdo underneath it all, and in that sense he shares something in common with Bond.

007 is a similarly deceptive character. Like Pattinson, he's a refined, handsome white guy with an urbane manner. But in the first Bond book, "Casino Royale," author Ian Fleming described him as a "blunt instrument." That element has been integral to the character since his inception. That is to say, Bond is much more than a posh boy with a licence to kill. He's damaged, troubled, maybe a little rough around the edges. Sure, his cinematic history has proved the character lends himself to interpretation, but the best Bond performances have integrated that dark side to some extent.

Pattinson could give us the best version of that to date. Remember that short film he made for GQ about his mounting anxiety over leaving his hotel room to get a hotdog? Something's up with this guy in the best way possible, and every role he's taken since then has been testament to that fact. From his lecherous, questionably-accented preacher in "The Devil all the Time" to his delightfully unhinged nineteenth-Century lighthouse keeper in "The Lighthouse," Pattinson has clearly been having a ball playing crazy (and that's not to mention some of his most Pattinsoniest performances in films such as "Good Time" and "The King"). He'll have to keep it under control for Bond, but 007 needs an edge to be interesting, and Pattinson has a wild unpredictability could be the best thing to ever happen to the character.

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of unknown actors being given the role. For Bond purists, such a thing is basically sacrilegious. For everyone else, it might just be the most exciting thing to happen to Bond since 1962's "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise.

Look, there's a chance Pattinson could be distracting as 007. Bond is a male fantasy come to life, and part of the series' success could well be attributed to the fact it's easier for audiences to project themselves onto relative unknowns. On the other hand, it only takes one Bond movie for an actor to become a major star, so there'll always be diminishing returns in that respect. What's more, I think it's fair to say we need big changes after the multiple duds that characterized Daniel Craig's last few years as Bond. The franchise was in danger of becoming less relevant than it once was, and casting a star of Pattinson's standing, in a movie directed by the similarly esteemed Denis Villeneuve is a way to remind people of the saga's blue chip status.

What's more, we're not talking about any A-lister here. Pattinson has proved time and again he has the ability to completely disappear into a role. So, what we're actually getting is an actor with the gravitas and appeal of a megastar who is simultaneously able to become a cinematic cipher onto which we can all project our fantasies of becoming the most lethal instrument the Secret Intelligence Service has at its disposal. As the first millennial Bond, and the first major star to take on the role, Pattinson could prove to be a master stroke of casting on Villeneuve's part.

There was a major turning point in Robert Pattinson's career whereby he seemed to throw caution to the wind and embrace the most challenging, unusual, and downright insane roles he could. In 2017, the year "Good Time" debuted, GQ exclaimed that "the new Rob Pattinson is defined by his willingness to go berserk or go home." Ever since then he has delivered back to back unforgettable performances that have seen the middle class London boy disappear into some of the most unique characters to appear on-screen in the last decade.

Part of it was an attempt to escape the shadow of the "Twilight" saga, with which he'd made his name. But his portrayals of these more off-kilter characters that came in the wake of his decision to recalibrate felt so natural and honest that it was like he was finally able to be himself, paradoxically by playing people so completely unlike himself.

What's even more impressive is that he hasn't slowed down since deciding to "go berserk." 2026 saw him deliver yet another electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire thriller "Primetime," in which he completely disappeared behind the mask of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson. Pattinson just can't seem to deliver a bad performance. Wild, sure. Unpredictable? Absolutely. But he's never been anything less than magnetic and seems incapable of being boring. That should be hugely exciting for James Bond fans.

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments but Robert Pattinson's ability to portray a debonair spy with a quietly simmering intensity was not in question. The actor played Neil in Christopher Nolan's thriller. A mysterious operative who helps John David Washington's Protagonist throughout the film, Neil possesses all the charisma of James Bond and even seems to have a bit of a dark side.

All you need to see to be convinced Pattinson has what it takes to play Bond is the scene in which Neil scopes out the freeport where he plans to steal a priceless art piece. As he's shown around the facility, Pattinson's agent simultaneously exudes a polite charm and a kind of palpable ruthlessness, smiling at his tour guide before staring intently at possible escape routes and security measures. You can feel the cogs turning as he looks around, with Pattinson managing to convey a real sense of Neil's thought processes. When he's told about the freeport's security system, which sucks the air out of a room within 10 seconds, he simply says "Blimey," an ironic understatement accompanied by a wry smile more than worthy of 007.

Surely nobody ever doubted Pattinson could play an urbane sleuth who looks remarkably sharp in a suit. But his "Tenet" performance hints at something more interesting. The brief moments when Pattinson's agent drops the charming facade and focuses his attention on various parts of the building's design convey a cold, calculating intensity that bodes well for a Bond with a truly dark side. Nolan's confounding thriller is an exciting proof of concept for Pattinson's Bond and his ability to exude both charisma and a striking cold-bloodedness unlike any 007 yet seen on-screen.

If you were told Robert Pattinson went to Eton and Oxford you probably wouldn't have a hard time believing it. He didn't, but it feels like he'd be very much at home in the public school boy milieu. That's interesting because while previous James Bond actors have managed to affect that kind of high-born aura, Pattinson is the first to just sort of have it from the get go.

He's an upper-middle class white Londoner with a Received Pronunciation accent and an urbane, sophisticated manner. Sure, he's also the guy who can't stop nervously laughing in interviews and who seems to run on pure anxiety most of the time. But there's no denying he has the sort of heritage you'd associate with Bond.

Roger Moore — the only other London-born actor to play Bond — had something similar, but undercut it with his famously tongue-in-cheek portrayal. Sean Connery was, of course, Scottish, Timothy Dalton was born in Wales, Pierce Brosnan is Irish, and Daniel Craig is from Chester in North England. Each of them brought something unique to the role, but of all the James Bond actors Pattinson seems like the first who won't have to work too hard at exuding the kind of aura we've come to expect from a character Idles frontman Joe Talbot described as a "murderous toff."

The newest Saturday Night Live episode aired last weekend, with comedian John Mulaney serving as Season 52’s latest host and Phoebe Bridgers performing as the musical guest. Unsurprisingly, the episode began with a cold open centered around recent events, and it centered on the controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. As part of that segment, Elon Musk was lampooned by the show again and, after he expressed disappointment with the impression, cast member Jeremy Culhane reacted.

SNL’s latest cold open sees the CIA gathering the U.S’ biggest tech magnates for a training session on not exposing secrets to potential operatives. The presiding official (played by Mulaney) speaks to Musk (Jeremy Culhane), Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes), Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline) and Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson). After Mulaney’s character unsuccessfully tries to make his case, Huang (played by returning cast member Bowen Yang) warns his colleagues using his own experience.

Ultimately, the real Elon Musk appeared to be less than impressed with the sketch, in which Mulaney’s character used venn diagrams to explain to the CEOs that a woman wouldn’t truly be interested in them without an ulterior motive. In response, Musk dropped a comment under the sketch on X and included a diagram of his own:

@nbcsnl lol https://t.co/7vw3wS9Jm3November 16, 2026

Throughout the sketch, Culhane’s Musk makes several random statements at the fictional briefing, one of which sees him compare himself to James Bond and another in which he tries to connect with Huang over their leather jackets. It’s because of those random asides that both the CIA official and even Huang use spray bottles on Culhane’s Musk. On X, after someone ranked the performances the actual SpaceX founder shared his take on Culhane’s impression, writing:

I’d give them maybe 5/10 for me. They need to try harder.

This isn’t the first time Musk has taken issue with an impression of himself on Saturday Night Live. Back in late 2024, the tech mogul – who also hosted SNL in 2021 – called out Dana Carvey for his take on him. The following year would also see Musk chastise Mike Meyers’ impression of him as well. The Tesla figurehead is far from the only star to ever take issue with an impression, as Kanye West disliked Chris Redd’s impression of him Also, Ice Cube was dismissive of Kenan Thompson’s take on him.

After this latest Musk impression, Jeremy Culhane took to his Instagram story to share a headline about Musk’s reaction. The Sex Lives of College Girls alum simply added the following caption to his post:

Reading between the lines, Culhane’s response seems to be a bit of trolling on his part. He may not have gone into detail, but it’s easy to get the feeling that he’s not too perturbed by Musk’s reaction to his performance. On the night of the taping, the actor’s performance also generated considerable laughs from the live studio audience. As for whether Musk might feel compelled to issue a response to the comedian’s social media post, that remains to be seen.

What can probably be assumed at this point, however, is that as long as Elon Musk remains in the news, this probably won’t be the last time he’s parodied on the long-running sketch comedy show. Viewers will ultimately just have to wait and see if or how further sketches materialize and for what reason. On that note, check out Saturday Night Live when it airs on the titular night at 11:30 p.m. ET amid the 2026 TV schedule. Episodes are also available to stream with a Peacock subscription.
